27.t: Leaving Warren for the Billy Clark carnival show and Pullman car
27.s: The Young family winters in Warren and leaves in March; Phillips joins on 15 April 1924 on a carnival owned by Billy Clark, living in a Pullman car and playing fairs.
27.q: : Oh yeah. Sure. They had a big apartment that they rented there for the winter. Yeah, they stayed there until about March. They left, went on a show, one of them little shows. And he told us we was goin' on a big show.

27.t: The carnival season ends in Palatka, Florida, then vaudeville
27.s: The carnival closed in Palatka, Florida in about November 1924 and Young moved into vaudeville.
27.q: We got on that show, and we went everywhere. We went traveling around. The show closed in Palatka, Florida.

27.t: Route of the first carnival tour
27.s: They went as far north as Indianapolis and played Kentucky and Tennessee towns, Roanoke and elsewhere.
27.q: Well, we played... Like, sent down to Kentucky to them little small towns. Lexington, Kentucky. Bowling Green, Kentucky. Knoxville, Tennessee. Chattanooga, Tennessee. Roanoke, Virginia.

27.t: How the carnival show worked: bally, spieler and band
27.s: Phillips explains the bally platform, the spieler or barker, and the band playing Running Wild to draw the crowd.
27.q: : See, what you do, you come out on a bally, all the people, all the show come out on the front -- the band, too. They got a big platform out there you come out on. You come out there and you play -- the band plays. You play something like maybe "Running Wild" or something like that ...…

27.t: Carnival versus band, and the Young family act
27.s: Sorting out terms, Phillips says the family had been in vaudeville before he met them, with Lester, Lee and Irma dancing and singing as an act.
27.q: No, I'm talking about the band. See, he had a band and a... See, this band picture I showed you wasn't in no show. We played dances. Went over the country playing dances.

27.t: Numbers in the carnival show: chorus girls, Lee, Irma and the midway
27.s: Phillips describes the chorus girls' dance numbers, the Young children's roles, Mrs. Young minding the money, and the other attractions on the midway.
27.q: Oh yeah, there were a lot of numbers. The girls used to dance "Way Down Yonder In New Orleans." The chorus girls used to dance.

27.t: Second day of taping; recap of the first tour
27.s: Resuming on January 27, Dupre recaps that the first tour ended in November 1924 and asks about the move to vaudeville.

27.t: Rehearsing a vaudeville show and the TOBA circuit dates
27.s: After the show closed in Palatka they rehearsed a week then played TOBA theatres, starting at the Eighty-One in Atlanta, a week per town, travelling by train.
27.q: Well, here's what the changes were. See, the show closed in Palatka, Florida, and we stayed there for a while. Then we got together a band and rehearsed. He rehearsed a vaudeville show. See, a vaudeville show was much different than a show on a carnival. He got that show together. Then we went on…

27.t: Who was in the Young show
27.s: Phillips lists the personnel: six chorus girls, the Young family, Pete Jones, Clarence Phillips, James Clark; the acts left behind.
27.q: the show, including the band and everything. They had a big band. I think it was about... Let's see, there was seven in the band.

27.t: Dirty Red, Shorty and David, and Grace Carter
27.s: Phillips tells about the performers: the blues singer Dirty Red fired in Tampa, the David and Goliath act, and singer Grace Carter who fell ill in Atlanta.
27.q: : A blues singer, yeah, and a dancer -- and a comedian; he told jokes and things. But he could sing the blues real good. He got fired. Mr. Young fired him in Tampa, Florida. That's where we left him, in Tampa.

27.t: The Lakeland minstrel show of early 1925 folds in Mobile
27.s: After vaudeville Young put together a tent minstrel show in Lakeland, Florida; it played Deland and Sarasota and folded in Flemington and Mobile.
27.q: No, she didn't get replaced. Because soon after that, we went down to Tampa, Florida, then we left Tampa... The show was getting ready to end then -- that's the vaudeville tour. Then we went to Lakeland, Florida. We stayed in Lakeland, Florida. There was a guy down in Florida had a big tent and a…

27.t: Leaving Willis Young for the DeParis show
27.s: Money got bad with Young, who gave them only eating money; Phillips, Pete Jones and James Clark left for Sidney DeParis Sr.'s show in Baltimore.
27.q: Flemington, that's where everybody was getting ready to leave. That's when I left Mr. Young; I was getting ready to leave him.

27.t: Why the minstrel show failed; Cootie Williams replaces them
27.s: Young's band was too small for a marching minstrel show, with Lee on drums; after they left he hired young Cootie Williams and others.
27.q: : Oh, no. We just marched on this minstrel show, and we'd make parades. You see, the thing about, why it didn't last long, because Mr. Young didn't have the kind of qualifications for the show. He's supposed to have a big band, like a 12- or 15-piece marching band for that show. He didn't have…

27.t: The DeParis show closes in Charlotte; winter back in Warren
27.s: The show closed in Charlotte in November 1925; the three went home and Phillips ran a six-piece band around Arkansas that winter.
27.q: Yeah. That's where I joined the show, but the show traveled around. We went everywhere, you know. We traveled around... That show closed in Charlotte, North Carolina.

27.t: The Great White Way show with a six-piece band, then Young sends tickets
27.s: Phillips's six-piece band joins Jim Thomas's Great White Way show, makes no money, quits in Memphis in 1926 and Willis Young sends tickets for them to return.
27.q: Yeah, bass horn. But he quit playing. He didn't play the bass with us. He was playing the saxophone well enough to play with us. He wasn't great, but, I mean, he was playing it well enough.

27.t: Young's gilley show and the move to Mrs. Young's big show
27.s: Young runs a small gilley show in Illinois while Mrs. Young runs a separate one; he hands his show to the barker Kitchen and takes Phillips and Pete Jones, the best players, to her show, which closes in Oklahoma in November 1926.
27.q: But anyway, we went up to this little show that Mr. Young had up there in Illinois. What we called a Gilley Show. That's one of them shows... It's a small show that travels... It don't travel with Pullman cars and wagons... Like a circus. You've seen a circus, how they travel. Well, that's the way…

31.t: Eubie Blake, Sissle, Miller and Lyles, and watching Eubie conduct
31.s: Whaley recalls Shuffle Along, Brown Skin Models, Miller and Lyles and Sissle and Blake, and Eubie's ritual at the piano.
31.ch: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
31.q: Eubie I met, I met him some show and we did -- oh, he was in Shuffle Along and 63rd Street and they went down to Baltimore somewhere and got stranded and they didn't do so good and come on back and then he came up to -- he come in the theatre. Irving Miller, Brown Skin Models.

31.t: Mr. Schiffman hires him as Apollo musical director
31.s: The Apollo's manager hired Whaley to orchestrate and rehearse shows.
31.ch: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
31.q: Yeah, he owned the theatre and he hired me as musical director. All I had to do was take the music that they brought in and orchestrate it and rehearse the girls with the producer, rehearse the show girls or the dancing girls.

31.s: Whaley and Donald Haywood rehearsed little Leslie Uggams, who went on the road with Cab.
31.ch: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
31.q: Yeah, little girl then and then she went with Miller's -- what's -- Miller had the chorus. She went with him.

31.t: The Nicholas Brothers and Sammy Davis's first Apollo date
31.s: Whaley directed the show for the Nicholas Brothers in Philadelphia and arranged for Sammy Davis and the Will Mastin Trio.
31.ch: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
31.q: Yeah, and he told me hey, you direct the show and let Mrs. Nicholas play and her husband would play the drums. I said I'm not going to direct no show. This is when I first started, so sure enough I directed this show and let Mrs. Nicholas play the piano and her husband played the

31.t: George Dewey Washington and Paul Robeson
31.s: Whaley met singer George Dewey Washington at the Lafayette and the Apollo with Leroy Smith, and says he never knew Robeson but saw him once.
31.q: Leroy Smith. He came here with Leroy Smith, at the Apollo Theater. And he would drink a whole glass of whiskey before he went on stage. Clear his voice, he said. And, oh, he could sing, George Dewey Washington, yeah. Great entertainer.

31.t: Vodery's Ziegfeld scores and Bert Williams in Boston
31.s: Whaley says Ziegfeld called Vodery the greatest writer, and recalls drinking with Bert Williams at an inter-racial Boston bar.
31.ch: Will Vodery and the road shows
31.q: Oh, Bert Williams, comes to me, Bert Williams, up in Boston. I used to hang out with him on Washington and Pembroke. We used to come there, Bert Williams used to come there and I used to hang out.

31.t: Bert Williams in blackface and Vodery's orchestrations
31.s: Hinton recounts Williams opening the Ziegfeld show with a gloved hand, and notes that Vodery orchestrated his records.
31.ch: Will Vodery and the road shows
31.q: Yeah, I know, Bill Vodrey was a big guy. To me.

31.t: On the road with 'Stopping the Traffic' and Dewey Wineglass
31.s: Whaley toured with dancer-producer Dewey Wineglass, who was hospitalised six months after fighting Elks in Pittsburgh, so Whaley took charge of the show.
31.ch: Will Vodery and the road shows
31.q: And we went -- where did we go? Not at Baltimore. Was it Baltimore we went? And he was made an Elk. And I told him to do everything they tell you, don't fight them. No, in Pittsburgh. That's right, in Pittsburgh. I said, don't fight him. Man, he started fighting them people and, man, they put him…

31.t: The TOBA circuit and Wiley Avenue in Pittsburgh
31.s: Hinton and Whaley explain the TOBA circuit, nicknamed Tough On Black Asses, and the show's stop on Wiley Avenue.
31.ch: Will Vodery and the road shows
31.q: this hotel, either the Top of the Hill or -- Wiley Avenue.

31.t: How Whaley first became a show director in Philadelphia
31.s: He explains Lee Whipper made him direct the show while Mrs. Nicholas played piano and Mr. Nicholas drums, and they straighten out the 1920s timeline.
31.ch: Will Vodery and the road shows
31.q: I used to conduct the show. That's -- I started when the Nicholas -- Mrs. Nicholas, she -- I was supposed to play the piano, see. I wasn't supposed to direct it. And I told the man -- he said, you go on and direct the show.

31.s: Whaley and Hinton try to recall TOBA acts such as Butterbeans and Susie, Flo and Cecil, the Whitman Sisters and the young performers who waited for critiques.
31.ch: Will Vodery and the road shows
31.q: I don't know. He may have been. There was a whole lot of people that was on that show, on that circuit. That was a big circuit, because when you come into town, the kids are right there waiting for you. I want you to see my act, see.

31.t: Apollo comedians: Pigmeat, Dusty Fletcher, John Mason and others
31.s: They list Apollo comedians, including Willie Green, Aphos and Estrelita, Pigmeat Markham's judge skit and Dusty Fletcher's 'Open the Door, Richard', and Whaley bar-hops after finishing a show.
31.ch: Will Vodery and the road shows
31.q: I would tell the bandleader at the end of the show, now, this is your show. Friday, we open Friday 5:00. I say, this is your show, I'm gone. And I would go up, hit every bar in Seventh Avenue up to 145th Street, turn over and go up St. Nicholas to 149th Street. Land up in Lucky Roberts.

31.t: Directing 'Red Hot Harlem' with Will Morrissey
31.s: Whaley describes Will Morrissey as white M.C. of the black revue 'Red Hot Harlem', the 'Penalty of Love' number whose two singers died, and Mae Barnes.
31.ch: Will Vodery and the road shows
31.q: White man. He would have a high derby, a silk hat. And he would come out before the show and sit on the steps and entertain. And then he says, Tom, you ready? I says, all right. He says, let's go. That was stopping the traffic.

31.t: Milton Berle and his mouthpiece Johnny Bigle
31.s: Berle came daily to hear Alan Drew, and Whaley says Berle's jokes came through Johnny Bigle, Clarence Robinson's partner and Berle's driver.
31.q: Milton Berle used to come to the theater, as I say, every day to listen to Alan Drew. And instead of Alan Drew cleaning up his stuff, like Milton did, becoming the greatest -- Johnny Bigle was Milton Berle's mouthpiece.

31.t: Alan Drew, the filthy M.C., and Redd Foxx
31.s: Whaley recalls Alan Drew's quick repartee, and they compare him to modern foul-mouthed comics such as Redd Foxx and Richard Pryor.
31.q: Alan Drew was an M.C. Milton Berle used to come up to the theater every day and sit there and listen to Alan Drew. The quickest repartee man in the world. But he was dirty, he didn't clean his stuff up. Milton Berle was dirty, but he cleaned it up when he went somewhere. Alan Drew was filthy. But…

67.t: Joining Sunshine Sammy's Revue and the TOBA circuit
67.s: He left the pit for Marion Hardy's band with the Sunshine Sammy revue, his first paid road job, and explains how TOBA actors were never paid on time.
67.q: Sunshine Sammy was one of the original "Our Gang" Comedy kids. He was a black boy there and he was a very fine dancer and so his father decided to take him out with a show.

67.t: Two days with a tent show, and circus parades
67.s: He split his lip on a tent show's constant outdoor playing and left after two days, and played circus parades in Nashville.
67.q: I did two days with a tent show from Nashville. I'd runup for the summer. I did two days with a tent show, I couldn't make it.

67.t: Snow Fisher, the cakewalker and sharp dresser
67.s: Cheatham knew Snow Fisher, a famous strutter in white pinch-back suits who did Shine and later became a big shot in Paris.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: He was supposed to be the greatest of the cakewalkers, yes. And that strutting, they call it the same thing, strutting. You know.

67.t: Comedy teams on the TOBA circuit: Bootsy and Pearl Swann, Hootan and Hootan
67.s: Cheatham remembers the husband-and-wife comedy teams who toured the TOBA circuit, some with Bessie Smith.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Oh, yes, I remember them well.

67.t: Johnny Hudgins' pantomime act played by the trumpet
67.s: Hudgins, a blackface mime, depended on a plunger trumpeter to voice his every movement; Cheatham played it in Europe with Wooding, and says a show needed a comedian.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Yes, it was sort of a preaching thing, yes. And I remember -- I think they started -- I don't know, I didn't know Johnny Hudgins Hodges until I went to Europe with Sam Hudgins. But I think they started that type of thing that Johnny Hodges was doing.

67.t: Tent show acoustics, lighting and backstage jealousy
67.s: Tent shows meant playing loud with no acoustics, lit by electric or kerosene lights, with jealousy among stars and chorus girls.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: No acoustics, that's why it was very hard on musicians to play tent shows. Cause you had to play so loud. All the time. Very, very difficult tent shows. And

67.t: Medicine shows with comedians, peppermint glass and snake oil
67.s: Medicine wagons carried strong comedians and minstrel acts, with white talkers selling cures, and were not considered old fashioned.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Well, you see, there was the big wagon that'd pull up -- in the back of the wagon they let the tail down and set up curtains in the back, you know, draped the back with curtains and they'd have a comedian. Now these comedians most of them were very good comedians, and dancers, and joke tellers. And…

67.t: The Kentucky coal-country tent show that split his lip
67.s: He lasted two days on a Kentucky tent show, too young for such hard playing, but values the experience young musicians no longer get.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Oh a lot of that stuff I did in Nashville, itself. The only tent show I played wound up in Kentucky. In the coal mines area. But I didn't stay because my lip split wide open. After a couple of days I had to leave, I just went back home. I couldn't play a -- that tent. I was too young and that was…

67.t: Entertainers Florence Mills and Cora Green
67.s: He knew of Florence Mills and Cora Green at the Deluxe but had no contact with them.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Yes, I heard of her being at the Deluxe, although I didn't, you know, it was just another performer, I didn't -- she didn't become real famous, I don't think till she came to New York with the show.

67.t: The big singing stars of Chicago in 1926
67.s: He names Alberta Hunter and Trixie Smith as the stars in 1926, plus Whitman Sisters singers such as Princess White.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Well the big stars were -- well now, let's see now. Course, we mentioned Alberta Hall and Trixie Smith was a big star then. During that time, too.

67.t: Chicago dance and comedy acts: Butterbeans and Susie, Brown and McGraw
67.s: Butterbeans and Susie were nightclub headliners in Chicago whose act Cheatham played many times. Louis Armstrong made the acrobatic husband-and-wife dancers Brown and McGraw famous by playing their whole act; later trumpeters were exhausted by it.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Well, Butterbeans he -- yes, they did a lot of night club work in Chicago, they were very popular, too. They were headliners. Butterbeans and Susie.

67.t: Dreamland singers and how tips were shared
67.s: George Dewey Washington and Walter Richardson sang at the Dreamland; tips were split among band and singers, unlike Alberta Hunter's reputed practice.
67.q: George Dewey Washington, and Walter Richardson, would sing at the Dreamland, like he would have them come in on weekends and sing. And they were very, very famous singers in Chicago at that time. They also sang at the Vendome.

67.t: Alberta Hunter as a young star at the Dreamland
67.s: He heard Alberta Hunter and Ollie Powers at the Dreamland, where she was a big, fine young entertainer.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: She was a big thing then, at that time, yes. Alberta was a big star at the Dreamland.

67.t: Singers George Dewey Washington and Walter Richardson
67.s: They were the two most popular male singers in Chicago, moving between the Dreamland, Vendome, Metropolitan and Sunset.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Well they were -- I thought I did. They were great singers. They were the two -- Walter Richardson. They were the two most popular male singers in Chicago at that time. And they sang at the Dreamland and they were singing at the Vendome Theater and Metropolitan Theater and other clubs, they'd go…

93.t: Dancing the Bugle Call Rag for Sissle and Blake
93.s: Green asks Noble Sissle's band to play Bugle Call Rag fast and dances with handsprings and a wheel step while Brown Skin Buddies performers and Tom Bailey watch.
93.ch: On the road with the Moores
93.q: Oh, that was Mr. Shelton Brooks. He was the composer of 'Some of These Days,' 'Darktown Strutter's Ball' and some other songs, and I think he liked me because I sang his song, 'Darktown Strutter's Ball,' you see, and my aunt had taught me a little step to do, you know, like to go off. See, that was…

93.t: Chinch and Ella B. Moore's TOBA revue
93.s: They tour Georgia on the TOBA circuit with the Brown Skin Buddies revue; Green recalls Ella B. Moore's singing and the show's performers.
93.ch: On the road with the Moores
93.q: -- so we went away, you see, with Chinch and Ella B. Moore, and we traveled throughout the South. We went to quite a few towns, like Gainesville, Georgia, and different places in Georgia.

93.t: Segregated seating played for comedy in the Nazarro act
93.s: Green explains the bit where Buck and Bubbles ask to sit downstairs while upstairs was for blacks; the interviewer asks if it parodied blacks and Green says it was authentic.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: Well, that was it. They were like children, you see, youngsters, you know, and it was based on this thing about -- like whites downstairs and the other, blacks

93.s: Green explains that variety shows had chorus girls and production numbers while vaudeville had only headline acts and was more expensive.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: Well, the difference is that variety shows are -- well, they had acts, but they also would have chorus girls, you know, and production numbers going on in a variety show. Where in vaudeville they only had acts.

93.t: Bert Williams' song Don't Help That Bear
93.s: Green recounts Williams' comic song about a hunter chased by a grizzly bear, which he saw in the Ziegfeld Follies with Will Rogers.
93.q: Yes. Well, the Bert Williams song, "Don't Help That Bear", is about -- there's a big hunter. He's famous for being a great hunter. He was out in some strange woods and of course he took his gun along. And he had been out there for the better part of the morning and the rest of the day, and when it…

93.t: The Kangaroo step and the Tacky Annie
93.s: Green lists new songs, demonstrates Chuckles' Kangaroo step from George White's New Shuffle Along and compares it with the Tacky Annie.
93.q: Yeah, well, it mostly consisted of introducing new songs, like, 'Scatting at the Kit Kat,' 'Born to Swing,' and 'Kangaroo,' that was the new dance, but it was mostly visual. There was an off-Broadway show, we introduced that song about the kangaroo, and Chuckles invented, created, a step. It was…

93.t: New Shuffle Along with Sissle and Blake
93.s: The new Shuffle Along featured Sissle and Blake and Buck and Bubbles; Chuck and Chuckles were on the bill as a separate act with a script.
93.q: Well, yes, you could say that. They were Chuck and Chuckles. We worked together, and when we became Chuck and Chuckles, our paths crossed, and that was one of the times. Our paths crossed, where we were on the same bill as Buck and Bubbles. But we were like a separate act at that time. We weren't…

93.t: Nat Nazarro and Sons, the balancing act
93.s: Green says Nazarro bought Buck and Bubbles' contract from Ramon Novarro and had been the bottom man in his own family balancing act.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: I don't think so, no. No, he bought Buck and Bubbles from Ramon Navarro, see, they were under contract to Ramon Navarro, that's what he told us, and he bought the contract, see? Buck and Bubbles used to make them little movies, you know. When they was children, you see.

93.t: Repeating the comedy as a little Buck and Bubbles, with mugging
93.s: Their own tap numbers were separate from the borrowed jokes; kids repeating the pair's lines and facial mugging made the audience laugh.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: Well, I mean Bubbles tap danced in his act, but we couldn't -- we had our tap dances, was what Nat Nazarro saw us do, like "Sweet Sue" and "Broadway Melody" and "Bugle Call Rag", you see.

93.t: The first performance with Buck and Bubbles was a sensation
93.s: Audiences did not know whether the boys were Buck and Bubbles' sons; repeating their jokes drew an immediate response in variety theatres.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: Well, it was an immediate sensation. Because it was a great surprise to the public. These little

93.t: More Buck and Bubbles stage routines and movie shorts
93.s: Green continues the piano-keys gag, then says Buck and Bubbles were stars from movie shorts and Our Gang comedies and the Nazarro act.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: what key are you in?" Buck would look at him and say, "Dark keys," you know. And he'd say, "Well, stay off the light keys." Then he'd play something else and he would sing, you know. He'd sing a song, like "There's No Greater Love," or something. But they had --

93.t: The oasis gag in the Nazarro family pyramid
93.s: Buck and Bubbles run through Nazarro's legs while he balances his sons and argue over seats; Green names Nazarro's sons and Nazarro's death.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: Well, they was arguing and say, 'Well, that's an oasis.' Well, I don't see no oasis.' Well, ask that man up there, and he's in the process of balancing all these five sons, you know, and they go chasing each other. I mean Buck would run through Mr. Nazarra's legs, you know, and Mr. Nazarra's…

93.t: Shelton Brooks coaches him in the wings
93.s: After applause, Shelton Brooks, standing offstage, tells him how to bow and to ask the bandleader for the Bugle Call Rag.
93.ch: On the road with the Moores
93.q: Now, I didn't have those bottle tops on my feet this time, you see, on the stage, but I was barefooted, see. The people wanted to laugh, you see, and I didn't think really that I could dance, you know. I was just learning these steps, you see. So a fellow was standing in the wings offstage, and as…

93.t: Buck and Bubbles' 42-minute act and the argue-over-the-speech encore
93.s: Green describes the length of the act and the encore where the two argue over who will make the speech.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: It was actually 39-1/2 minutes, but they had an encore, which was 2-1/2 minutes, you understand? Like they'd come out and bow, and they says -- they would both say, 'Ladies and gentlemen.' Then they would look at each other and one would say, 'Go ahead, you make the speech.' 'No, you make the…

88.t: Early show business: father takes the children on the road
88.s: Lee says he was in show business as long as he can remember, left New Orleans at about five after his parents separated, and sang and danced as a child.
88.q: But now getting back to the carnival, if you want to know what I was doing with the carnivals then, which you may want to know, I was a blackface comedian.

88.t: The TOBA circuit and its stars
88.s: The family worked the TOBA circuit through the South and Midwest, sharing bills with Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith and others, where Lee really learned to dance.
88.q: Let's see if I can get it chronologically for you. Let's see, after we left the carnivals, this is just what I can remember, you know? That we were on the TOBA circuit, which is ...

88.t: Carnival life as a child: the Midway and Hey Rube
88.s: He describes carnival midways, side shows, the Hey Rube fight cry, hustling for dimes, and seeing nearly every state by age 13.
88.q: Oh, well, I remember the minstrel shows, you know, like you're a kid and they had the 'Midway' -- if you're not a country girl, you may not know about the Midway.

88.t: How minstrel shows worked; Sophie Tucker selling her book
88.s: Tent minstrel shows ran full performances with 10-12 acts and sold photographs; he compares it to Sophie Tucker selling books in Miami in 1956.
88.q: : Well, Minstrel shows were one big tent. They were tent shows -- tent minstrel shows, and there was a large tent, like, not as big as the Big Top with the circus, you know, but it was a big tent, and I think it would seat, like, 3 or 400 people, and that's a lot.

88.t: The Young kid act that nobody wanted to follow
88.s: The father's act featured Irma, Lester and Lee singing and dancing; Lee as a comic made the music stop for thrown coins.
88.q: Yeah, well, they always had comics, you know, because it was slapstick comedy, you know. But they had a lot of acts that were similar, but it's who was the best, and the business -- you will hear people talk now about shows and who wants to open and who wants to close the show, you know? But when…

88.t: The all-black minstrel show on a white carnival and the Sword Lady box
88.s: Their minstrel show was the only black attraction on the carnival; his sister was put in the sword box illusion.
88.q: Nope, just the minstrel show. Just the minstrel show -- but on carnival, everything was white but the show that we were in, you know, and it was all black -- it was a minstrel show, that's what it was called.

88.t: Lee as a child blackface comic
88.s: He describes his blackface costume and makeup as a small boy in minstrel shows and carnivals.
88.q: Uh huh, and the carnivals. Yeah. My sister has a picture someplace; as a matter of fact, my son has a picture. I must have been around that tall.

88.t: Minstrel show structure, TOBA blackface comics and Al Jolson
88.s: He explains the interlocutor and end-men layout, says black comics on TOBA wore blackface, and mentions later recording music for The Jolson Story.
88.q: Okay. Well, you see how they're in a semi-circle. A semi-circle, and they have the interlocutor -- and he's like the straight man. Now, the funniest people in the minstrel show, and it's just like the chorus girls, you know, how the chorus girls dance? The better dancers were always on the end --…

88.t: Lackman and Carson carnival, Ida Cox and Blind Denslow
88.s: They confirm the carnival name, discuss Ida Cox on minstrel shows, and Lee recalls the blind dancer Denslow.
88.q: No, you never do. But see, when you're that young, somehow you catalog these things and you do remember them, you know. And I don't know if I told you about -- there was a team -- someone would remember -- on one of the minstrel shows we were on, the man's name was Blind Denslow, and now I never…

88.t: Lee as the comic, Lester as straight man, Irma leaving music
88.s: Lee played the comedian while Lester was straight man, and Irma stopped playing and went into singing and dancing.
88.q: Right. Yeah, she didn't play any more, and then she started dancing and singing and she worked quite a few places.

88.t: More on Bill Robinson and Lee's poor memory for years
88.s: He says he cannot date events, only incidents, and recalls Robinson running backwards faster than others ran forward.
88.q: No, see, that's the difficult thing about me. Now I can tell you about situations and incidents, you know, but I don't have a clue to the year then, and if you

88.t: The Brownskin Models show and how Red Callender came west
88.s: Lee corrects the Brownskin Review to the Brownskin Models, a dancing and singing show, which brought Red Callender to the coast.
88.q: I think it was the Brownskin Models. That's the show that I remember -- it was the Brownskin Models, and the Brownskin Models -- oh gosh, if I could only think of this lady's name; a beautiful woman; beautiful brown skinned woman, and she had all these beautiful brown skinned girls with her; she…

88.t: Los Angeles theatres and the Follies' black pit band
88.s: Irma worked at the Burbank Theatre; Lee recalls a black orchestra in the pit of the all-white Follies, where a white dancer was fired for speaking to a musician.
88.q: For instance, when we first came here after I told you about the Apex, and then after I stopped doing that and I started playing music, she used to work downtown at the Burbank Theatre; there was a Burbank Theatre down here on Main Street -- you know, Los Angeles really had a lot of places for…

231.t: Going with the carnival and refusing Ringling Brothers
231.s: The owner would not take underage Buck; Bubbles describes the all-white carnival with a colored show and says he turned down Ringling at 13.
231.ch: Louisville, Buck and the carnival years
231.q: show -- the carnival -- I went with the carnival for maybe two or three months, maybe a little longer. And I went traveling with the carnival --

231.s: He names the carnival Superior Shows and Kid Fox, and describes its colored singing and buck dancing.
231.ch: Louisville, Buck and the carnival years
231.q: wanted me and I wouldn't go, this carnival that was in Louisville, when I went to Indianapolis I said -- I went there with a fella after we got the act together -- we got the act together -- see the name of Buck and Bubbles together, then we played at the state fair and all --

231.t: Black comedy acts of the 1920s: sketches and blackouts
231.s: He recalls military and hospital sketches, blackouts and Pigmeat Markham at the Apollo, without remembering jokes.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: Comedy like sketches they had, blackouts they had, they did military sketches. It's hard to tell you the comedy acts they had, but it was really terrific comedy.

231.t: Buck and Bubbles as pioneers; Bert Williams and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.s: He says black performers got on big stages gradually, that Bert Williams was the first Negro in the Follies, and that dirty gags were unthinkable then.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: No, they weren't, there were no performers on the stage, man. Are you kiddin'. You're talking at the time that the only person, negro on the stage at that time was like Bert Williams and -- what's the name of that act --

231.t: Knowing Bert Williams and Jack Johnson; minstrels and plantation shows
231.s: He met Williams and Johnson in New York; earlier black performers were in minstrel shows, not major theatres, and Negro acts were a godsend to vaudeville.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: weren't in the business. I hope you can get the understanding that these people were on the stage before me but where were they on the stage? Where were they? If you're talking about a theater, you're not in any theater in the united world unless you are at the Palace or the Paladium as of today…

231.t: Getting into Lew Leslie's Blackbirds in 1929
231.s: The lawyer tells them to wait for a better case against the Canadian manager, and Lew Leslie hires them with Ethel Waters and the Berry Brothers.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: But anyway, getting back to when we come out of Canada and come back to talk to the lawyer and the lawyer says he's got to get something better or a better platform to go against the manager than that. I says, okay, I'll wait. So we waited. Went into "Blackbirds" after that in 1929.

231.t: The carnival's minstrel format and a cow-and-watch joke
231.s: The black troupe did a minstrel show with an interlocutor and two end men; he recounts a joke and says it needed two people to deliver.
231.ch: Brawls, the Ink Spots and boyhood recollections
231.q: That's the straight man that asks all the questions. He's called the interlocuter. And two end men, interlocuter and they have the rest of the people fill in like a chorus, you know, we all sang together, we all had jokes together.

231.t: The show Dancing Around with Harry Steppie
231.s: A white revue with comedian Harry Steppie, chorus girls and Alan Walker; Buck and Bubbles were the only black performers.
231.ch: Solo years, marriages and the Canadian party
231.q: No, it was a show. No, they had a comedian, chorus girls, straight man in the show, the comedians would do jokes and they'd do sketches, like that, you know.

231.t: How the Buck and Bubbles spot fit into Nazarro's acrobatic act
231.s: Nazarro's acrobatic act ended with a missed trick and a gag that brought on Buck and Bubbles; Bubbles says they never worked blackface after Louisville.
231.q: only thing he did was acrobatics. He was an understander, he had a top mounter. He thought a one-man trick and missed the trick, that's when he introduced us.

231.t: Nazarro's company and how he introduced the act
231.s: Nazarro was an acrobatic understander with a little partner; Buck and Bubbles did their own act on his bill for over five years.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: No, not Nazarro -- Nat Nazarro and his company. He had a boy, understand that worked with him. He had an understand that worked with him, there were no brothers. He hired a little fella that he could pick up and throw up and down to do a Hawaian trick or flag him up, he'd do tricks. I never seen…

231.t: Vaudeville versus cabaret and the theatre circuits
231.s: He distinguishes after-hours cabaret from daytime and nighttime vaudeville, and says only theatres ran in chain circuits like Orpheum and Loew's.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: Well, the cabaret is after hours, it's in the night time after hours and vaudeville is a daytime and nighttime situation. You do different shows in the daytime and different shows at night. But the vaudeville has a bill of variety acts, one after another. Night clubs don't have that. Now, you've…

231.t: Blackbirds closing, the Berry Brothers and Jig-Saw Jackson
231.s: The show folded after 12 to 14 weeks; he describes the Berry Brothers' strut dancing and the roller-skating, contortionist Jig-Saw Jackson, and how good the show felt.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: Jig-Saw Jackson. They were a dancing team, a trio, a dancing trio, three brothers, called The Berry Brothers. They were some dancers, too. Did a number called 'Papa Dee-Da-Da' used to strut to it, you know. It was terrific, yeah. And I used to laugh, it would be so interesting to watch them work,…

231.s: In vaudeville you follow other acts and do just an act, while in pictures you play a part.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: You follow acts on a program of vaudeville and in the pictures you do -- you play a part. See, that's the difference. You don't play no part on the vaudeville stage. You just do an act.

80.t: Joining the show: stranded in Chicago, South Bend and Omaha
80.s: A con-artist manager talked his brother into letting him tour; the show played a failing theater near Chicago, got stranded in South Bend, and sewed costumes on the way to Omaha.
80.q: It was okay. It was -- because this guy, I found out later, he was world's best con artist, and he asked me if I would go with the show, could I go. I said I don't know, you have to talk to my brother. So he met me then. He outtalked my brother naturally, you know, and I wanted to go, and he said,…

80.t: William Benbow's Get Happy Company and the cold train to Texas
80.s: The show was Ben Bow's 'Get Happy Company'; Benbow gambled away the money and rode in comfort while the troupe starved in the baggage car.
80.q: Yeah. And he had, you know, he had a big diamond horseshoe pin he used to when he keep the money, and he find some -- he called it finding some fools, to play poker? And they were waiting for him.

80.t: Confronting Benbow for back pay in Austin and leaving the show
80.s: In Austin, after Benbow's empty promises, Autrey locked the door, threatened to throw him out the window, got some cash, and slipped away to join a carnival.
80.q: Ah, well we played Galveston, Houston, we played all over Texas, all over towns. Still didn't see any money. So when we got to Austin, that's where I grew up. I became a man. I -- he'd been calling us in and talking to

80.t: Bandleader of the Florida Tip Top Shows carnival
80.s: He led the band for Billy Wonder's Florida Tip Top Shows, playing ballyhoo and show music with seven to ten men.
80.q: Yes, it was -- yeah. Well, you had to double on and off. In other words, you go out and make bally-hoo to draw the people in.

80.t: The big-chopped stranger who outplayed the carnival band
80.s: A shabby young cornetist with huge lips came to sit in, and amazed the classically trained band by playing anything without music.
80.q: I'm -- I guess even now, a stranger comesin, he wants a job, he wants to sit in, or join the band. The guys try to make it -- some guys want to make it tough for them, you know. Say who is this guy? So well, we'll lay something on him and see what he knows, see what he can do. And they make it hard…

80.t: Trombone Jones, the drunken Fisk graduate
80.s: He tells of a brilliant, perpetually drunk trombonist in the carnival band who had graduated from Fisk and who corrected the college men from under the wagon.
80.q: Yes. Yes, I was. Because I was the leader, became the leader of the group, and I think we had a pretty good band, and let me think. Who else was there? Oh, that's what I meant to mention. It was a trombone player on this -- Jones, he was on this job. We called him Trombone Jones, and he was a -- he…

80.t: Hearing other traveling shows: George Gillam and Amos Gilliard
80.s: He went to hear visiting bands; he remembers trumpeter George Gillam, trombonist Amos Gilliard, and a white Whiteman-style bandleader who featured a black player.
80.q: Yes, well that's it. Every time you get a chance, the other traveling bands and shows would come in town, go to see and hear them -- and meet them.

80.t: The road show 'Hello Lois' in Jacksonville
80.s: After the carnival he took his band into Pet Jensen's road show 'Hello Lois', a theater revue of chorus girls and comedians.
80.q: Well, let's see, I think I came -- oh, I joined a road -- what they call a road show, and still in Florida, in Jacksonville, Florida, after having my own band I got the heck out of town, I joined the show, and I played the band, took the band over there, and I was with Pet then.

80.t: The Black and Tan show formed in Boston
80.s: Back east he joined a Black and Tan TOBA show assembled in Boston, led its small band, augmented by local players, and starved as usual.
80.q: We came back east and we heared of what they called then at that time a Black and Tan show, which was forming, getting together in Boston, so we went, we came to Boston to meet and join these people, and anh, the show was pretty good. And --

80.t: The Howard's fourteen-piece band and playing Ben Hur for the silents
80.s: The Howard job grew to a 14-piece pit band playing overtures and whole silent films; his ability to read got him the job.
80.q: It was, a doggone good job. Come to be finally we had a 14-piece band there, and was playing heavy because see Caroline was conducting, and we -- I played (finger snapping) Ben Hur in that theater.

80.t: The only music he heard in Alabama
80.s: Before Pittsburgh he heard only minstrel shows, circuses and marches, then dance bands, and recalls a white bandleader trombonist whose son became a movie star.
80.q: Oh, yes. Heard things like dance bands. Just a minute, before I leave Alabama I'd like to -- no, I heard him later. I'm sorry. Because I want to -- his son, from his son's a movie star. He played trombone. He played trombone himself, had his own band, white.

80.t: Eubie Blake conducting the Standard Theater pit band
80.s: He worked under Eubie Blake in pit bands, including Philadelphia's Standard Theater, where Eubie insisted musicians watch his baton and took the first drink for his dime.
80.q: I know Eubie -- I know Eubie very well. I worked under Eubie in pit bands, lots of times. Yeah, he was directing the band, directing the orchestra, and oh, Eubie used to say -- we used to -- man, in Philadelphia, particularly, and Standard Theater. We had about oh, ten or twelve piece band. I…

453.t: Presbyterian school at Hot Springs and his brother joining the circus
453.s: Their mother sent the boys to a parochial school in Hot Springs in 1912; his brother ran off to Ringling Brothers, performing a side-show act with Mantan Moreland.
453.q: And my brother, he stayed at school awhile, so when school was out he didn't come back to school and he didn't come home, so we wondered where was brother. I

453.t: Playing from the porch of a Charlotte theater for Hawaiian films
453.s: The college band played Isle of My Golden Dreams and similar numbers above a theater for the movies and earned a little money.
453.ch: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
453.q: Well, no. The only time we went -- like this time like this fellow like I tell you, T. B. JOnes, he would carry the band up and they had this movie was showing some big picture for the Hawaiian -- some Hawaiian picture. So he had the band come and sit out on the -- something like a porch like over…

453.t: Leading the band in a Pigmeat Markham show
453.s: He led the band for a small touring show starring Pigmeat Markham around the South until it disbanded back in Durham.
453.ch: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
453.q: Well, no. I stayed in Durham for a good little while, then we got -- I got with the show playing -- leading the band with a little show starring Pigmeat Markham.

453.t: Playing in a medicine show band
453.s: A four-piece band played fast marches while a doctor sold a dollar-a-bottle tonic, staying three to four weeks in each town.
453.ch: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
453.q: No. This was just a -- this man -- he would sell medicine and he'd have -- to my idea, I think he would have a lot of chicken entrails in a bottle, in alcohol or something like that, and he would tell them that

453.t: Escape artist, comedians and the medicine show's break-up in Cincinnati
453.s: He describes the show's acts, including an escape artist who expanded his chest against the ropes, and how the show broke up after Greensboro and Cincinnati.
453.ch: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
453.q: And now, here's -- we had -- what we would do -- we had a nice little show. We had comedians and an escape artist. We had a fellow -- we had some big men would come up and tie that fellow -- tie him and he would get loose, just like that. They would come up there to tie and when they tied him we…

453.t: Playing the minstrel show with J. L. Cronan's carnival
453.s: The trombonist wired a 42-car carnival, and Randolph played ballyhoo in town to draw crowds, nearly laughing at the barker's closing line.
453.ch: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
453.q: I sent her back home in Durham. Well, the show broke up and after that we went to look in the paper and we saw J. L. Cronan's Carnival Show where they needed a band. So, Holt wired them -- the trombone player wired them, so we went there and we joined them in Burlington, North Carolina. And that's…

453.t: Taking over the band at Watkins's theater in Durham
453.s: He returned to Durham to lead the band at a theater owned by Watkins for three or four months before going home to Arkansas.
453.ch: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
453.q: I took over that show there and I played there for awhile. Didn't last any too long. Then what I did, I went right back home after I left -- after I played -- I guess we stayed in that theater about three or four months. Then I went back home to --

453.t: Playing silent pictures at the Criterion Theater from cue sheets
453.s: Taking over Shirley Clay's theater job, he read overtures and Sam Fox folio music matched to film cue sheets.
453.q: Singleton, he was something! Well, then I played around and giged around there for awhile and then after I ran into this fellow -- dead now, Shirley Clay, he asked me if I wanted his permanent job. I told him yes. He said, 'Well, I'm going to New York,' he says, 'and you can have this job playing…

453.t: Touring with the Pass in Review unit of the 1933 World's Fair show
453.s: Glaser sent Randolph and Sunset men to join Leo Salkins's Pass in Review revue, which toured Iowa and the state with sixty white performers.
453.ch: Sunset Cafe, Pass in Review and rebuilding the band
453.q: We stayed there and played a while, with the band. So finally, Joe came and says, he says, "I want to pick you, Randolph." He says, "I want to send you to Milwaukee to join the unit of the --" they had a unit of Passing Review of the World's Fair of 1933.

453.t: Leading the small stage band at the Indiana Theater in 1941
453.s: He took the band onstage at the theater at 43rd and Indiana after the singer Lamille, with saxophone, drums and piano, sometimes himself playing both trumpet and piano.
453.ch: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
453.q: I took the band in the Indiana Theater -- who did they have there? A girl by the name of Lamille and she left. I played under her, played under Lamille. This was -- I don't remember those dates back then. Let's see, all right. I have to go to thinking about residence, then maybe (that was still,…

453.t: Playing head arrangements for touring acts at the Indiana
453.s: The theater band backed acts from the Oriental Theater and Chez Paree, reading music only sometimes and otherwise following a sung melody.
453.ch: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
453.q: We would get acts there, maybe say like an act would be booked down at the Oriental Theater, so you know it must have been a long time, because whenever the Oriental Theater been open, see, and we were getting acts from Sullivan's show, that would be booked down there. We would get acts from the…

453.t: Hippodrome Theater in Danville: Walter Morrow's trio and TOBA shows
453.s: He played sideman in a three-piece theater band for touring shows, using arrangements by Eddie Heywood Sr. and backing TOBA acts like the Whitman Sisters.
453.ch: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
453.q: So, I didn't know where the boys went. One of the boys went one way, so I got a job playing at the Hippodrome Theater there.

72.t: Walking gent with A.G. Allen: tending the band coats
72.s: Hired as a walking gent to hang up and dry the six-piece band's red parade coats, travelling by Pullman car.
72.q: So I got an opportunity to join this minstrel show. But I joined the minstrel show, but I wasn't... I wasn't able to play drums, because I was... They hired me for a walking gent, to hang the coats up on the bushes or the trees when the band would make the parade and go downtown...

72.t: Joining A.G. Allen: pay and life on the Pullman car
72.s: The show was a mile and a half from home; he started at three dollars a week with room and board on the car.
72.q: When I started... The first minstrel show, which was (?)... The first minstrel show was about...oh, say, about a mile-and-a-half from my home. I could walk there, you know. So I was talkin' with the man, and he said, "You want a job?" I said, "Yeah." He said, "I'll make you my walking gent." When…

72.t: A.G. Allen the man; parades and touring North Carolina
72.s: Allen was easy to get along with, wanted a good show; parades drew crowds; the tent show played North Carolina towns and needed parade permits.
72.q: He was very easy to get along with. He'd never bother you about nothin'. All he'd do, he wanted to put on a good show. Put on a good show and receive that money. They used to come... I think during that time to see the show was... I think it was fifty cents, or seventy-five cents, something like…

72.t: Leaving Allen for the Old Kentucky Minstrels
72.s: After about four months, still not playing, he moved to the Old Kentucky Minstrels in the Carolinas to move up toward New York.
72.q: I wanted to move up. A.G. Allen just played right down South all the time. But I wanted... All my main ambition was to get to New York. But I didn't come to New York with no minstrel show. I picked the Old Kentucky Minstrels down in South Carolina or somewhere down in there. That's the last one.

72.t: Joining a road show in Birmingham (TOBA-type circuit)
72.s: Explains 'road shows' as touring revues of musicians and entertainers, which he picked up in Birmingham.
72.q: Then I got to this...you call it... Well, you call it, TOBA is the road... We called them road shows. I got this show down there in Birmingham, Alabama -- this road show.

72.t: Becoming the drummer on the Old Kentucky Minstrels
72.s: When the drummer fell ill he played parade and show, was offered the job at six dollars, and describes life on the car.
72.q: About the same thing. But I got the (?)... Before I left... I think before I left the Old Kentucky Minstrels, I was able to play drums in the parade. That's when the drummer taken sick, and they asked could I play...could I play the parade and the show? Well, I had confidence in myself. I told…

72.t: Old Kentucky Minstrels: management and South Carolina towns
72.s: One man was manager and boss; the show played mostly South Carolina, and the band began to play more modern, swinging material.
72.q: Well, during that time, a little bit later... Later the (?) started. The Old Kentucky Minstrels started to play a little bit more modern stuff, and swing more. There was more outlets(?), you know.

72.t: Where the band sat; piano or banjo in minstrel shows
72.s: The band sat on a platform before the stage, with a piano if there was a girl singer.
72.q: Well, the minstrel performers... We had a stage. And the band would be right in front of the stage, down on the floor. They had a platform on there, but not as high as the stage -- a platform for the band. Sometimes they'd have a piano, and sometimes they just used a banjo in place of the piano.…

72.t: Clarence Muse and the Charleston Dandies at Birmingham's Gaiety Theatre
72.s: He quit his show in Birmingham, joined Clarence Muse and the Charleston Dandies, and was housed by the theatre boss at the Gaiety.
72.q: I quit(?) that show in a joint... I was playing drums in parades. The manager...the boss of the theatre must have liked what I was doing. The ..(?).. said, "I ain't got too much for me(?). If I (?) with you, I've got a theatre, so I can put you in the theatre. I'll give you forty…

72.s: Describes blackface comedians, bands in minstrel shows including Freddy Jenkins and the DeParis brothers, pay, Pullman cars and railroad siding fees.
72.q: Well, they called it "Emmett Till had to stay on his own bottom." That means when you're working in a minstrel show, you've got to be able to take care of your own self and do your work, make the people happy. Because they call it entertainment.

72.s: He also played in the pit for Eubie Blake's shows with changing tempos, alongside Sweatman's stage act.
72.q: My first time with Wilbur Sweatman, I went back with Dave Nelson. And I went back again with Eubie Blake. Because Eubie Blake had a fourteen-piece band.

72.t: Eubie Blake as strict bandleader; the Pie, Pie Blackbird film
72.s: Blake was busy and strict; the band toured theatres and made a short film with Nina Mae McKinney.
72.q: He wanted me to take some drum solos, which I did. The drum solo would run around about six or seven minutes, very short, you know. I didn't have too much time.

76.t: Ethel Waters, the Lyric Theater and John Robichaux
76.s: Marge says Ethel Waters claimed she brought Zutty out of New Orleans; Zutty says she taught him the Charleston at the theater. He worked the Lyric with Robichaux only after leaving the Cadillac, and after the Navy.
76.ch: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
76.q: Now Ethel Walters she tells, brought she's told it several times that she xrxkxxxxxuxgxkxx out of Zutty New Orleans. She liked him so much at the Lyric Theater. She didn't bring Zutty out of New Orleans.

76.t: Seeing Count Basie and Lovie Taylor's dancing in St. Louis shows
76.s: In St. Louis they saw Count Basie with Gonzelle White on the burlesque wheel, plus Rose Marie and Chu Chin Chow. Jasper Taylor's drumming in Joe Jordan's band backed the soft-shoe dancer Lovie Taylor.
76.ch: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
76.q: We saw more than that. This other fine show on the Burlesque Wheel with Jasper Taylor was playing drums. Jasper Taylor was in Joe

76.t: Big bands and shows versus small groups
76.s: Dance notes Zutty's early career was in big bands and shows, harder work; Zutty recalls the Connie's Inn show and how his Lyric Theater experience helped him catch dancers' moves with the ratchet.
76.q: That show in Connie's Inn was really something, boy. Then all that happened in New Orleans while playing at the Lyric Theater with old man Robichaux. See, I had a little experience on that see? And that's why I could catch guys in different ratchet. You know, like cats used to make a split and pull…

76.t: Leading his own band at the Lafayette Theatre
76.s: Zutty led his own band in a show at the Lafayette, with Tom Whaley conducting instead of Donald Haywood, Bubber Miley on trumpet and Gene Anderson on piano; Nina Mae McKinney hit an actor with a gun that jammed.
76.q: You see, it was my band. That's when (Nina May McKinney?), she was in the show. And (Plessey?), it was a spot where (Nina May McKinney?) was supposed to shoot this guy. And the gun wouldn't go off. So she walked over and hit him over the head with this pistol and blood started flying everywhere…

76.t: The Berry Brothers act at the Paramount with Tommy Ladnier
76.s: Zutty and Tommy Ladnier played the pit for the Berry Brothers act at the Paramount, then Brooklyn and Providence, and Joe Jordan used the union delegate threat to get the locked pit doors opened.
76.q: Ladnier did, we did that at the Paramount Theater. And we played two weeks here at the Paramount, then we went to Brooklyn and played two weeks. Then we went to Providence, Rhode Island.

76.t: Clarence Jones's band at the Metropolitan Theater with Louis
76.s: With Jimmy Noone at the Nest, Zutty joined pianist Clarence Jones at the Metropolitan Theater, a movie house where he and Louis did an act and he wore a dress for a comic number.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: We did a tune once that if I can't play first fiddle I aint going to play no fiddle at all. And I'd have on a dress and everything.

76.t: Ralph Cooper's band at the M and S Theater
76.s: Marge recalls the M and S Theater band in new blue uniforms, led by the dancer Ralph Cooper who could not hold a saxophone, with Henry Goodwin and Gus McLeod on trumpets; it rivalled the Apollo and was soon renamed the Harlem.
76.q: But in the last band I was always with Zutty. That's why I know what happened got to go with him every place and they made Ralph Cooper the leader of the band and I don't know what big gig you all were going on because you had these beautiful new uniforms and it was night you were rehearsing.

76.t: Ethel Waters and the four-in-a-bar Charleston; Tim Moore
76.s: Zutty says Ethel Waters taught him the Charleston singing James P. Johnson's tune; he could not manage two in a bar, so played four in a bar. Tim Moore's boxing act with a midget is recalled.
76.ch: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
76.q: Yes indeed. She sure did. Because she was singing that James P. Johnson, 'Charleston, Charleston.' You know she'd get right, I was down in the pit, but she was up on the stage and she would (SOUND OF CLAPPING). But I couldn't make it with two in a bar. So when I put that four in a bar that made…

76.t: Two years at the Lyric Theater among the vaudeville acts
76.s: Zutty played the Lyric about two years, knowing Ethel Waters, Bessie Smith, Bruce's grocery store tab show, Butter Beans and Susie, and a dancer compared to Bojangles.
76.ch: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
76.q: Oh gee, about two years I guess, think because I knew Ethel Waters and Bessie Smith and Bruce and his grocery store.

76.t: Norman and Arlene Selby's blackface Louis act
76.s: After the Renaissance with Vernon Andrade, Zutty went to Philadelphia and Chicago with Norman and Arlene Selby, whose act had Norman impersonating Louis Armstrong on trumpet.
76.q: That's right. That's right, yes. And right after the Renaissance I went to Chicago. I went to Philadelphia with Norman and Arlene Selby. She used to do a Louise Cook dance and he made up black face.....

76.t: Getting the John Robichaux job at the Lyric Theater
76.s: Robichaux heard Zutty from outside the Cadillac and hired him; Willie Jackson and another rehearsed him on the chorus-girl kicks. The Lyric stood at Burgundy Street and shone a light on him.
76.ch: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
76.q: Well, it went on quite a while until old man Robichaux was standing outside listening at me play and that's how I got the job.

76.t: The Follies Bergere in Chicago with Sally Rand
76.s: In Chicago in 1933 Zutty played the Selby act in the Follies Bergere floor show, sitting in the band beside George Wettling, with Sally Rand and Joe E. Lewis in the show.
76.q: Well I went back with Arlene and Norman Selby. We played in the Follies Bergere. That's when Sally Rand made a big hit at the Fair. See, because I played with Irving Rothstein, Rothstien, Rothchild or somebody. His band was playing the show. You see, a big show. They had Joe E. Lewis was in the…

377.t: The Gonzel White vaudeville show and being stranded in Kansas City
377.s: Basie confirms touring on the Keith circuit with Gonzel White's show, which broke up and left him stranded in Kansas City, though he gives few details.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: Vaudeville act. (inaudible) the show pieced together, you know. He's got (inaudible) little things and the little bits that (inaudible) putting together. It's (inaudible) whole thing all about. But what (inaudible), it's true.

377.t: Why he wanted show business: travel, carnivals, excitement
377.s: Basie says he loved the show and had always wanted show business, travel and carnivals more than being a musician as such.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: That's it. I just wanted to get down and I wanted to travel. I used to want to just do everything, wanted to be a part of show business. When I was a kid, I mean, there was very little that you could see (inaudible) theaters and maybe some of the acts would come to the theater, you know, and then…

377.t: Playing a silent movie theater in Kansas City
377.s: He played for silent films in Kansas City from cue sheets, liked it, and the hours were roughly 7:30 to 10:30.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: (Inaudible), just liked it. It was something that I (inaudible), just wanted to do, and got a chance to do it, I liked it (inaudible) for a while.

377.t: Music as the road into show business
377.s: A somewhat muddled exchange in which Basie says music was how he got into show business and that he wanted to be part of it, traveling and with a carnival.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: When you read this thing, (inaudible) then you'll see right where (inaudible). See, everything has to happen at the beginning and before you get to this hotel, you have to get here.

377.t: Trying to recall the name of Katy Crippen's act
377.s: Basie says Katy Crippen was a woman who sang and led a small act, and tries to remember what her group was called.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: Would know about what it was called? I don't know. It might just have been -- it had to be something like Jazz Hounds House or --

377.t: The Hippety-Hop show versus Katy Crippen's vaudeville act
377.s: Basie explains Hippety-Hop was a big burlesque-style show, while Katy Crippen's was a vaudeville act of a few players; he was with her act on the Hippety-Hop bill.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: Oh, no. Beg your pardon now. I'm ahead. Katy Krippen was not in that show. Katy Krippen and Hippety-Hop, two different shows.

377.t: Sonny Thompson, the Gonzel White show and leaving it in Kansas City
377.s: Basie identifies Sonny Thompson as a drummer and confirms two years with the Gonzel White show, which ended in Kansas City around 1927, and a bout of illness.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City

377.t: Disputing the 'honky-tonk piano player with a touring vaudeville show' quote
377.s: Basie says he would not have used 'honky-tonk' and that it should be a show, not vaudeville, which only had acts.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: Well, we must have been talking about something. It had to be we'd be talking about the show or something like that, if he's saying we didn't have any names in

377.t: Playing silent films at the Eblon theater
377.s: Kuehl reads that he played for silent films at the Eblon theater; Basie says all but the passion plays are his words.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: All but "the passion plays" are mine.

377.t: The Big Jamboree folds in Kansas City and he is stranded
377.s: Basie says the Gonzel White show, called the Big Jamboree, was stranded in Kansas City, which led to his illness and later joining Walter Page.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: Yeah. Now, you see, it's so much in that, well, this is all true, that is (inaudible) all true. But it's -- so much is going to be added to that, you see, because that show was very instrumental in getting back to Kansas City the second time. I recall that first time, I didn't (inaudible) -- didn't…

377.t: The Whitman Sisters, and first returning East with Bennie Moten
377.s: Basie says the Whitman Sisters ran a road show that was not important to him, and that he came East again only with Moten's band and later again with his own in 1936.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: With her? No, that's a road show. They had (inaudible). I mean, they actually -- I don't know whether I just have any room in my book for her -- them or not, see, because they -- I mean, they haven't meant that much to me. You know what I mean, it's -- as far as anything (unintelligible) they would…

386.t: Joining the 'Get Happy' TOBA road show with Leonard Reed
386.s: In 1927 he joins Happy Donovan and Travis Tucker's TOBA show to Houston, and Clara Donovan hums melodies and stomps tempos for him backstage.
386.q: And really go far away? In 1927 Leonard Reed, who was a dancer, who used to be very, very close to Joe Louis, was in Dallas with his wife. We were naturally at the Ella B. Moore Theater. A show came to town, a traveling show in the TOBA. You know about...you know...well, the TOBA was a circuit…

386.t: Out-playing Herschel Thomas on 'Suitcase Blues' in Houston
386.s: At an after-hours club Price plays Herschel Thomas's own solo and wins the room, then repeats it when Herschel follows him to Galveston.
386.q: He was a blues player. Herschel and I were friends. And Herschel...women liked him, you know...so he always had two or three women following him around, so after the show one night we went to this after-hours club and when we got into this after-hours club, he tried to show me up by telling…

386.t: Down the TOBA route: Shreveport and Mobile
386.s: The show moves through Galveston, Shreveport and Mobile, where he meets Lannie Scott, George Lewis and Professor Campbell.
386.q: Shreveport is where I first met Lannie Scott and met George Lewis and...let's see...Professor Campbell had the band, in the Star Theater in Shreveport. And from Shreveport we went to Mobile, Alabama. And all the time, Danny, each week we were meeting different people. Different shows of 20 people,…

386.t: The TOBA as a training ground in respect and fidelity
386.s: He describes the TOBA circuit's route and the code of looking after sick or stranded performers, and recalls helping James P. Johnson and Willie the Lion later.
386.q: It was a very interesting training ground. It was like a Who's Who in America, you know, in black America because if they were anybody, from Georgie Williams and Bessie Brown to Bert Williams to Ma Rainey to Trixie Smith to...well, Ella wasn't around in those days, you know...you know this TOBA was…

386.t: On the TOBA singers were the stars, not the bands
386.s: He explains that blues singers and comedians were the attraction, soloists had little room, and territory bands played elsewhere.
386.q: You know, Danny, during those years singers were the principals. You don't think that Coleman Hawkins could take his tenor saxophone player and go out and stand in front of Butter-Beans and Susie and be the star. He was just another musician in the background. Maybe they'd let him play a number.…

386.t: Danville, Virginia: Boisse DeLegge and the Huberts
386.s: Returning to the TOBA story, he tells how Joe Hubert was lured away from Boisse DeLegge's show and punched in the eye.
386.ch: Marriage and the end of the shows
386.q: Yeah...well, I spent almost a year in Chicago. What had happened was, when I left the TOBA after the conclusion of that ill-fated tour, we went to Atlanta and...well, I've yet to tell you how I got my first wife, you know...we ll pick up there.

386.t: Failed comedian in Washington and Christmas 1928 back in Dallas
386.s: After shows break up, he is fired as a comedian for forgetting lines and eventually returns to Dallas by Christmas 1928.
386.ch: Marriage and the end of the shows
386.q: Well, a show came through, and as I said, they always need people. So we got on the show and went from Pittsburgh to Washington and then in Washington that show broke up. Then we got on another show and went from Washington to Baltimore and back. We just...nothing was consistent, nothing was real,…

386.t: Broadway shows and managing Sidney Bechet's affairs
386.s: He recounts shows including Tambourines to Glory and Clash By Night, and managing Bechet's business.
386.ch: New York, Philadelphia and Harlem nightlife
386.q: I began playing more in New York and then I did Tambourines to Glory with Langston.* I did Clash By Night on Broadway with Tallulah Bankhead. I did another thing called The Last House on the Left with Irish Owen ...he was a playwrite and a producer. The show was so bad, until the actors asked him…

386.t: Friday openings at the Apollo Theatre
386.s: He describes the crowds for Duke's opening, the Pearl Bailey show, the comedians and Buck and Bubbles.
386.ch: New York, Philadelphia and Harlem nightlife
386.q: Friday morning. That's the opening day. Friday morning to Thursday night. And oh, the hustle and bustle, and guys getting in, you know, to get a seat. Guy want to hear Johnny Hodges' new solo that he played on "Mood Indigo," or whatever in the hell it was. Everybody was there for Duke's opening…

386.t: Tallulah Bankhead bars Billy Rose and the show closes
386.s: Bankhead bars Rose from the theater after a dispute and the show closes.
386.ch: New York, Philadelphia and Harlem nightlife
386.q: Now, we rehearsed this show; we tried out in Detroit; we played Philadelphia; and one day in New York when we were getting ready to open, Tallulah Bankhead went up on the right side of the theater and there was a scene where that you could not see her, you know, for that's like a fleeting moment.…

137.t: What the 101 Ranch show was like
137.s: He describes the 101 Ranch Wild West circus with Indian tribes, staged raids, a big arena and its last show at Yankee Stadium.
137.ch: Circus shows and learning to voice
137.q: It was a big circus, with -- like the Ringling Brothers Show, only they had a bigger ring, because in some of the acts they had three or four tribes of Indians.

137.t: The white parade band and the black minstrel band
137.s: The show had a big white parade band and a 14-15 piece black band that was cut to nine for the night minstrel show.
137.ch: Circus shows and learning to voice
137.q: Yeah, and they set it up out in the and they had two big bands. They had a great big band and they had about 15 pieces of black band, and then they'd break the black band down to about nine pieces for the minstrel show at night.

137.t: March books, minstrel repertoire and the blues that turned the tide
137.s: The band played ragtime and march books until Durham's blues from the wagon changed it; he left the circus around 1921 at Yankee Stadium.
137.ch: Circus shows and learning to voice
137.q: That's when I left the circus. They went to Europe from here. I played at Yankee Stadium and I didn't go any further.

137.t: Black band musicians and the circus going to Europe
137.s: Uncertain whether the black band went to Europe; he names trumpeters Amos White and John Mason and a fine drummer.
137.ch: Circus shows and learning to voice
137.q: We had a terrific trumpet player there named Amos White. John Mason, from -- who was the leader. Those guys could do anything with a trumpet.

137.t: Circus wagons, horses, elephants and moving the show
137.s: Band wagons were horse-drawn, an elephant called Big Jimbo pushed stuck wagons, the show travelled on its own trains; Durham wrote jazz licks for the minstrel wagon.
137.ch: Circus shows and learning to voice
137.q: They didn't march and play. They had big wagons for it, the big band wagons, the big band. There was about 30 pieces in that big white band, see. And they played on a truck and then we come along last with the minstrel show, with a few comedians on it, and that's -- see, we could play Sweet Georgia…

137.t: Playing the pit for the show with his brothers
137.s: The band played the overture and show in the pit and had to read; Joe, Earl, Roosevelt and Eddie were all in the band, but only Joe was in the 101.
137.ch: Circus shows and learning to voice
137.q: There was nobody in that but my brothers. The one on the piano was there, and the clarinet player was there. Joe and Earl and Roosevelt and myself, all four of us were there.

137.t: Touring with the Alabama and Georgia Minstrels at 16 or 17
137.s: When minstrel shows came through town they hired him on trombone; Edgar Battle was in the shows and trumpeter Harry White could play jazz.
137.q: See, but I -- later years, when I was about 16, 17, I got on the circuit, the shows -- see, I was with Alabama too, but I was just remembering one time (inaudible) I was with that and the Alabama Minstrel and the Georgia Minstrel.

137.s: He stayed two warm-weather seasons, touring all over the States.
137.ch: Circus shows and learning to voice
137.q: You know, as long as the weather was warm, right up until --

137.t: Mamie Smith's 7-11 show and Battles' band
137.s: After the 101 he went with the Goldberg Brothers' 7-11 show with Mamie Smith in a nine-piece band led by Edgar Battle with Herschel Evans; he wrote what the band could play.
137.ch: Circus shows and learning to voice
137.q: So the last engagement we played was at the Orphan Theatre, I believe, in Newark, New Jersey, and that's when the show started.

66.t: Leaving professionally with Buzzin' Harris's TOBA vaudeville show
66.s: A touring show's pianist fell ill; she memorised the whole show from the owner's humming and played that night. She toured Ohio and Indiana for two months with comedian Brodson (Buzzin') Harris's weekly TOBA vaudeville.
66.q: talent show then. The first time I left really professionally is when a show came to Pittsburgh and the pianist, something happened to him so the Western Union boy hdd delivered a wire to the owner of the show. The owner told him, "My goodness, I need a pianist. I've got to go out..." He said, "I…

66.t: John Williams and his combo join the Harris show
66.s: John Williams, whom she later married, joined the Buzzin' Harris show in Cleveland with a combo, won her mother's confidence, and had a trombonist, Sylvester Briscoe, who played with his foot.
66.q: : John Williams - I later married him, you know, my first husband - joined up with the Harris Buzzin' Harris show in Cleveland.

66.t: Her role with the Harris show and the clowning of the jazz-band era
66.s: She played for the show, danced when a chorus girl was short, and did comic piano tricks like playing with a sheet over the keys; the 1920s combos clowned a lot.
66.q: No, no special, all I did was I played for the show and when they were short a chorus girl I'd go up on the stage and dance. I never did a solo but we did a combo. You know that was during the era in the 20's of the jazz band, you know, small combos and all they did was clown. A lot of music was…

66.t: Joining John Williams's combo and how she felt about him
66.s: She joined John's six-piece combo in the Harris show to get away from home. She admired him as a person but did not love him enough to marry, and the group toured small towns in Indiana, Ohio and Oklahoma.
66.q: : I don't remember if I just played piano and that's all for the show. I don't remember having a drummer or anybody then.

66.t: Carnivals and circuses with Doc Cheatham
66.s: The group played circuses and carnivals, which she hated, with Doc Cheatham, Briscoe and guitarist Joe Williams, scraping by on little money.
66.q: During this period we played for circuses and carnivals and that is the worst life that anybody could ever - oh, my goodness. I thought about that and I just shivered in bed once because these roustabouts - you call them that? - they are terrible... Doc Cheatham, good trumpeter, did you ever hear…

66.t: The Pearl Theatre in Philadelphia and the double piano
66.s: Billed as Blanche Calloway at the Pearl Theatre, Andy put her on a small piano beside Jack on a Steinway. When Jack fell ill she took the big piano and was kept.
66.ch: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
66.q: : in Philadelphia. Andy decided to use me for that theatre date, so he put me on a little miniature piano and had Jack on a big Steinway. So I was on the left of it, a left-handed stage, and he was over to the right. One afternoon Jack got sick or something happened to him. Steeple used to bring…

66.t: Florence Mills, Ziegfeld and the Harlem theatre scene
66.s: At 14 to 16 she met Florence Mills through Jeanette. She relates Ziegfeld's way of handling singers, and describes Mills as sweet and delicate, like Josephine Baker.
66.ch: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
66.q: Yes. Florence Mills was a very good friend of Jeanette's. Jeanette used to take me everywhere with her. See I was very young and she wouldn't dare to leave me alone.

66.t: Moms Mabley, John Mason and Bojangles at the Tree of Hope
66.s: She met comedians Moms Mabley and John Mason, and Bill Bojangles, who could run backwards as fast as others ran forwards.
66.ch: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
66.q: I think Josephine was younger. During that time I met, in fact I played for Moms Mabley. Her name was Jackie Mabley then. And John Mason - oh, they were the most fabulous comedians. They were the same on the street. John Mason had a little baby just could barely talk. He'd stand on the street and…

66.s: Mills was a dancer and singer, in the Ziegfeld show 'Poor Little Blackbird'; she was sad when Mills died.
66.ch: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
66.q: Yes, 'Poor Little Blackbird' or something like that show, that's when I met her.

382.t: Seeing touring shows, bands and TOBA acts in Pittsburgh
382.s: As a girl she saw road shows, dance bands, Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey, the Elmore Theater and midnight shows.
382.q: shows. We had Hot Chocolates and Black Birds to appear in Pittsburgh. So I mean, I got to see these productions when I was young.

382.t: Lil Green and the black theater circuit
382.s: On the Benny Carter tour: the Lincoln, Howard, Apollo and Royal theaters.
382.q: Oh, sure. When I was out on the road with Benny Carter that one tour, Lil Green was on the road, too. They followed us. Every place we played, they were right behind us.

382.t: Edith and Lena Wilson, Adelaide Hall and Black Broadway
382.s: Lena is Edith Wilson's sister; Edith was the original Aunt Jemima.
382.q: Yes, she is Edith Wilson's sister -- Edith Wilson who is the famous artist from the early -- about the turn of the century and I saw Edith -- Edith is now appearing with the Black Broadway production.

382.t: A Louisville concert and vaudeville dates
382.s: A one-off jazz concert in Louisville; she was mostly doing concerts and vaudeville.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: Just one performance. I went down there. It was sponsored by the local newspapers and the local NAACP, and they had quite a show. They had Harlan Leonard Band, and some local acts.

382.s: She appeared in Ken Murray's revue in Hollywood.
