382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: No that was out in Hollywood. It was a review that Ken Murray did. I was out there in the review for about ten weeks in 1944. He had a long run out there. Ken Murray at the El Capitan Theater. It was something similar to the "Hell's A-Poppin'" that was done here on Broadway in New York. In fact,…

382.t: Frank Schiffman and the Apollo Theater circuit
382.s: Schiffman owned the Apollo and the next stop was the Howard Theater; the black theater circuit.
382.q: It probably was part of a larger syndicate, because Schiffman -- the syndicate, I supposed, were part of the eastern, what they called 'seaboard' chain of theaters.

382.s: Her first vaudeville engagements at Loew's State and the variety acts on the bill.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: first engagements at the vaudeville house at the Loews State. I went in with my arrangements. I had maybe about eight or nine songs and I thought I was going to get a chance to sing them all and the manager would come back and say, you got twelve minutes. So I had to pick out three or four good…

382.t: Footnote on Avis Andrews and Cab Calloway
382.s: Hughes adds that photos show Avis Andrews, who sang with Cab Calloway and in the Harold Arlen show 'Great Day'.
382.ch: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
382.q: Well, yes, I got to know Avis Andrews naturally after I came to New York but I think I mentioned earlier that on an occasion when I was supposed to appear at the Apollo Theater and they had the bill as John Kirby and Maxine Sullivan, I didn't show up for that engagement and Avis Andrews sat in --…

382.t: Vaudeville at Loew's State and a Benny Goodman concert in Boston
382.s: She played vaudeville houses repeatedly and was an added attraction with Goodman in Boston, carrying her own arrangements from Columbia.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: Yes, I did vaudeville. I used to be in Loew's State at least four times a year. And I was on a theater tour, more or less. You know, I was booked out of New York and I guess I must have been out on the road about two years doing vaudeville theaters. You know, jumping from one place to another. And,…

758.t: First road show in Sharon, Pennsylvania
758.s: The band could not read the smeared music, the show was saved with a simple opener, and the stranded players gave ten-cent shows in a storefront.
758.q: : And we got out... The first crack out the box, we got stranded. We got through... Well, to start off with... This is the funniest thing about that gig. We were rehearsing, rehearsing tunes and all that, and then when we got there, they had music. But the music was like the music where... It ain't…

758.t: Youngstown dance and getting hired for a carnival
758.s: A five-dollar dance gig in Youngstown led to a party where Roy played Hawkins's Stampede chorus and was offered a job with a carnival band.
758.q: : Then we finally got a gig. Some guy wanted the band to go to Youngstown to play a dance, you know. And the money was nice. I guess it must have been about five dollars each. That was nice then, you know. Heh... He said, "Do you fellows want anything to eat before you go?" So the cats said, "Yeah,…

758.t: Carnival band: hiding that he could not read
758.s: Roy struggled outdoors, was mocked by the piano players, was tricked into revealing he could not read, and ended up playing drums for the same twelve dollars.
758.q: : But they still didn't know I couldn't read. And they didn't know I'd never played outdoors! I had a (?) little old pea-shooter that had never been cleaned out, you know. They had bought this arrangement on "Stampede" and was playing oom-pah behind me, you know, and it was so loud you couldn't…

758.t: Rock Dinah show and being cut by a singer
758.s: Roy fronted a road show band, was slashed with a razor by a singer, and refused to press charges against her.
758.q: : trumpet player, but I wouldn't stay nowhere. Because any time the money got strange or some of this stuff... But this thing... I got back on...

758.t: Meal tickets and the ice cream carton
758.s: On the road, Roy learned to grab food and filled a carton for later, learning in Kansas to reach for dishes.
758.q: : And I stayed with that thing until... Oh, we had some real evil experiences with that. We went down there... Let's see, where did we go first? We went down to Oklahoma...no, Missouri. You used to have meal tickets, you know. And I was always one to devise some way to get what I needed. And I had…

758.t: Roy Elliott and His Palais Royal Orchestra
758.s: As bandleader he was renamed Roy Elliott and featured East St. Louis Toodle-O with a gold tin can.
758.q: : Yeah. They changed my name, naturally. They've been doing that since time began. If you're the leader of something, you have to have a different name. Your name don't fit, you know. So they called me Roy Elliott and His Palais Royal Orchestra of New York.

758.t: Bergie Hines's relatives' show in Oklahoma
758.s: Describing the road show in Oklahoma, a skit that had to be changed to a minstrel look, and the hostility to the pit band.
758.q: : Yeah, man, let's see... Oklahoma City and then we went to... Oh, we had this little road show, too; you know, this was a road show. And I'll never forget, man. We had... Do

758.t: Three carnivals and how they worked
758.s: After Rock Dinah he worked three carnivals with their own Pullman, privilege and gambling cars; musicians were nobodies.
758.q: : Oh yeah. Rock Dinah was no carnival; that was a road show, a TOBA show. And then I was on Greater Sheesley, and then... I was on three carnivals, Beckmann and Garrity(?) and C.A. Worthen. Yeah.

758.t: Big To-Do's band and Saturday parties in Mississippi
758.s: He played drums with Big To-Do's five-piece and at weekend parties with gambling behind a sheet while the show owner was away.
758.q: : So I had two little bottles of senso(?), you know, for ...(?)... He must have never seen them; he took those. He just took them. Then a wagon came and trucked all of my stuff. Because I had the drum set; you know, I was playing the drums. I got to the job right quick! I was with ...(?)..., we…

29.t: Patsy, the daughter who dances and choreographs
29.s: Howard says his stepdaughter dances and sings; Mrs. Howard says Patsy assisted Leroy Prinz at the studios and began at sixteen at the Cotton Club.
29.ch: Sue and Patsy Howard in show business
29.q: Yeah, she -- I think she was 16 when she first started with (unintelligible) at the Cotton Club.

29.t: Patsy on the Ellington revue Jump for Joy
29.s: Patsy describes dancing and assistant choreography in Jump for Joy: the cast, three-month run and its social-consciousness numbers.
29.ch: Sue and Patsy Howard in show business
29.q: Well, there was Nick Castle, who had -- he was formerly with Paramount Studios and Columbia different Studios, but mostly with Paramount.

29.t: Patsy at Paramount and Small's Paradise
29.s: Patsy worked as an assistant to Leroy Prinz at Paramount, and left for Small's Paradise in New York, 1944 to 1946.
29.ch: Sue and Patsy Howard in show business
29.q: Yes, I was more or less with Leroy Prinz when he was at Paramount and I was assistant dance instructor to he and his brother.

29.t: The Show Boat revival with Paul Robeson
29.s: Patsy and her mother worked in a Los Angeles Show Boat with Paul Robeson.
29.ch: Sue and Patsy Howard in show business
29.q: In the stage play of "Show Boat," she was one of the original cast, she and Paul Robeson and she played the part of Julie, sang "Can't Help Loving that Man of Mine."

29.t: The WPA Hot Mikado and Janet Collins
29.s: Patsy describes the WPA production Hot Mikado, assistant choreography and ballerina Janet Collins.
29.ch: Sue and Patsy Howard in show business
29.q: That was in the thirties, '38 or '39, something like that. And as I said, when they had the WPA, they wanted to put on Hot Mikado and of course, they had to put the girls in the WPA in order to have a show, because at that time they only had like laborers.

29.t: Sneaking in to hear Bert Williams and Black Patti
29.s: At nine he sneaked into the opera house for Bert Williams; Mrs. Howard recalls seeing the singer Sissieretta Jones, called Black Patti, in Steubenville.
29.q: Oh, now I remember the first time that I saw her. See, I was born in Atlanta. And the first time I saw her I think I was around 11 or 12 years old. --oh, her career-- And (inaudible) let's see, I think she had traveled all round -- round 1927 -- it was in the 1920s actually. But, oh -- at that…

29.s: Collette asks about a minstrel show and a San Francisco band; the Howards cannot date it.
29.q: I was tryin' to think of the name of that last band I played with up there, San Francisco.

29.t: Patsy's club shows in Los Angeles

77.t: Touring with a pianist and dancer on the Keith circuit

77.t: "Struttin' Time" at the George M. Cohan Theater

77.t: Male impersonators: Seymour and Jeannette, Florence Mills
77.s: Jeannette of the team Seymour and Jeannette was a classy male impersonator, as was Florence Mills, whose outfits Lou Leslie kept immaculate.
77.ch: Struttin' Time, chronology and Chicago singers
77.q: Oh, well now, I tell you the male impersonator that was popular in the early '20's, a girl -- it was a team called Seymour and Jeannette. Jeannette was a male impersonator, but he was Seymour was --

77.s: Downtown stars like Tucker and Jolson came up to hear them; Twinkle Davis had legs, Goldie Crosby, Mamie Carter and Nellie Carr could sing or dance.

77.q: -- that was when the Apollo was-the Apollo, was-the show of Broadway, I mean one of the theaters of Broadway, and you said the Apollo Theater on Broadway, you had made history, you know. 77.t: Cora Green, Bricktop and the Panama dancers
77.s: Cora Green had an in-between voice, Brick talked her songs and danced; Hunter had to dance in Show Boat in front of the chorus.
77.ch: Struttin' Time, chronology and Chicago singers
77.q: what I mean? She had an in between voice. Everybody on that floor was a different type, had different type voices. Everybody on each one of the floors upstairs and downstairs had different type voices.

58.t: Leaving Chicago on the road with Charles Taylor's show and carnivals
58.s: When Chicago slowed, Punch went on the road three years with Taylor's show, then did carnival tours each summer.
58.ch: Road shows, carnivals and New York

58.s: Punch runs through Bronze Mannequins, Jerry Jackson's Cavaliers, Royal American, Silas Green and Jimmy Straits before coming home late 1956.
58.ch: Road shows, carnivals and New York

58.t: Chorus girls, floor shows and comedians

58.ch: Jelly Roll, Leonard Reed and Chicago mixed crowds
58.q: Now, there's one thing I've never told you about. He had a fellow named Leonard Reed. I don't know if you've ever heard of him. Can't place him now. Well, he's a show producer. He used to be a tap dancer a long time ago. Real light boy. But he got up on one of the best shows in Chicago ever was…

58.t: The Robichaux show band at the Lyric Theater
58.s: Punch recalls the Lyric midnight shows and how the Robichaux band moved from march to ragtime to jazz.
58.ch: Opening and New Orleans trumpet players
58.q: Yeah, I used to play at the Lyric Theater. I used to go there all the time. Midnight shows? Before I left. Yeah, they used to have midnight shows. That was before I left New Orleans, way back there. I was here around 22, 23, 24. I started left in 27. Well now, Robo Show, did he feature much jazz at…

58.t: Working for the Clyde Beatty circus
58.s: Punch describes two summers with the Beatty show playing parades and a colored revue, and playing Maryland.
58.q: Big stone there and blowed everything down. Blowed the top down on us man. I used to get the parking lot and cut my way through. Where was that? Up in uh somewhere in Wisconsin. Yeah I worked for two summers I mean. Two summers. What kind of stuff you played? Oh we had a college show on there. Oh?…

58.q: Yeah. No, I wasn't there when she died. I had been playing with her and I left. When she was taking sick, we left her home, see. And she died about a year after that. Oh, after you left her.

58.s: Punch describes the Lyric's changing weekly shows and the late Midnight Rambles for white patrons.

They played the Lyric Theater. They played the Lyric Theater and it was there a whole week. Who all would come to the Lyric?…

108.s: He played Broadway shows including the long-running 42nd Street and explains why he kept turning the pages despite memorising the music.

108.t: Noble Sissle lets him into Broadway: 'Alive and Kicking' and 'Guys and Dolls'
108.s: Sissle released Wilder to do his first Broadway show, a revue, and then 'Guys and Dolls', followed by 'Silk Stockings' and 'A Most Happy Fella' before ABC.

108.t: Nightly boredom and Broadway job security
108.s: Fighting boredom by playing as on opening night; Broadway offered more security than traveling bands.
108.q: I had never done it before, except when I did Alive and Kicking. That was the first time. What you had to fight was boredom, because you get to the point where you have nothing – there’s nothing to really keep your interest as keen as it should be, and you tend to get a little lax. But then you…

108.t: Seeing shows built on the road
108.s: He watched Most Happy Fella and Silk Stockings develop, with Art Lund replacing a singer.
108.q: Yeah. It was a lot of fun to see that, because you saw it begin – it begins to develop, and you’d see there were spots where it got weak and where it didn’t seem as if it was going anywhere. 103.t: On the road in 1930 with shows, doing everything, show-business discipline
103.s: In 1930 he plays drums, piano, sax, sings and dances with shows; he recalls show people's strict discipline and the Billboard blacklist.
103.q: Yes. But I wasn't quite sure whether I played drums or piano because sometimes you'd catch me, I would be playing saxophone. Sometimes I'd be singing. Some places I'd be dancing. 103.s: Jones recalls meeting Butterbeans and Suzie in Birmingham and describes the big black acts, Eddie Lemons, Ida Cox, and the record Hinton and he made with her.

103.s: He praises Manzie Campbell as the greatest drummer, who could roll perfectly with his left hand, and describes the sideshow of Collier's Shows.

103.s: Jones describes Crack Johnson, an Oklahoma drummer resembling Jack Johnson, who played in the big tent with Sousa.

33.s: DeDroit says being commercial meant playing polkas, Yiddish music and five-four Greek music, and recalls touring Ohio and Pennsylvania as feature trumpet with Arnold Johnson's orchestra.

14.s: Love describes Kimball's wife the pianist, their job in Hot Springs and return to the Hippodrome in Shreveport, while Love worked at the Star.

14.s: Talk about an entertainer called Rock from Memphis who played solo slide whistle, with comparison to Abbey Foster and Pigmeat Markham.
14.q: He used to play solo whistle too, you know, play solo whistle, one of them slide and whistles. He was good at that. I'm trying to think of somebody. The fellow was an entertainer, it was with us, was named Rock. They called him Rock.

14.t: Kersands' jokes, the English queen, and the impostor John Johnston
14.s: Love recalls Kersands' chicken joke, how he made a solemn queen laugh in England, his spending and drinking, and a big man in the show who was mistaken for him in Mississippi.

101.t: On the road with Ida Cox and her Darktown Scandals

101.s: Distinguishing carnivals from medicine shows and minstrels; the jig show at the back of the midway.

90.t: The Silas Green show and Bessie Smith

98.s: DeMichael raises a three-tier ranking of Chicago black musicians; Saunders corrects it with the Regal, Metropolitan, Grand and Monogram theatres, Dave Peyton, organists, and TOBA.
98.ch: Childhood, first drums and the hustling years
98.q: No, the Regal didn't start until -- yeah, well, it started in '28, right, in '28. But it was just the thing, it wasn't enough to take the demand of how many black musicians there were.

98.t: George Kirby's rise from dishwasher at the DeLisa
98.s: Kirby imitated people in the basement; Mike put him on stage with Leon Washington's arrangements and he never looked back.
98.ch: Regal Theatre and the changing music scene
98.q: No, what he actually did was, he went through the basement there where the dressing rooms were, and he was always imitating somebody. And so, Mike said, 'we'll put him on the stage, we'll put him on the stage. We'll get together with the Red there, we'll put him on the stage.' So Leon wrote the…

98.t: Joining Curtis Mosely's band in the Harlem Scandals revue
98.s: After the Walkathons he joined Mosely's 13-piece band in a road show with chorus girls and acts, his introduction to show work, playing Chicago theatres and the Midwest.
98.q: It was low level, but right after I left the Walkathons, and this was about 1933 I left the Walkathons, pardon me, then I joined a big show, a big revue, called the Harlem Scandals. And there was a road show, and we travelled. We travelled all over.

98.t: Name acts and a proving ground: Eckstine, George Kirby, Lurlene Hunter
98.s: Shows had up to 16 girls and five or six acts; Billy Eckstine, George Kirby and others got their start there.
98.q: Well, they were name acts -- they were name acts like today, with guys like Billy Eckstine, But, see, it was a proving ground for all these acts. They were young. See, we're talking about the '40s and things like that then, you know. Billy Eckstine, he got his start there, and George Kirby was --…

98.t: Four years with the Walkathon bands, and Red Skelton
98.s: He joined Ira Coffee's small band at a Denver Walkathon and travelled with it through Minneapolis, Atlantic City and Kansas City; Red Skelton joined as comic and MC.
98.ch: Childhood, first drums and the hustling years
98.q: Yeah, so we went to Denver, and they had the Eligious Garden, I think it was,that they had the Walkathon, and I went to work there with a fellow with a fellow named Ira Coffee. He was a piano player. And I stayed with the Walkathon for about three or four years.

13.t: Playing silent-film scores for Erskine Tate at the Vendome
13.s: Describes the theater pit, picture scores, hand-signal themes and fast cuts between numbers.
13.q: pictures. Played all kinds, played jazz, classical, overtures, and quite naturally, we had to play for the pictures, so we had to play -- they sent out a release -- when they sent a picture out during the week, they'd send a score with it. And you had to have all these different numbers in the…

13.t: The Regal stage show; leaving for the Grand Terrace in 1931
13.s: Describes the band doing stage presentations behind chorus girls and acts, under M.C. Fess Williams.
13.ch: Joining Earl Hines and the Grand Terrace
13.q: Yeah, on the stage it was under the direction of -- oh, I can't think of his name. He was an M.C.

13.t: Dave Peyton's band at the Regal
13.s: Peyton led from piano; stage by Fess Williams; mostly newsreels and stock arrangements.
13.ch: Part Two: theaters and the Chicago scene
13.q: Let me see. I can't remember who did the arranging. We didn't have many arrangements in Dave Peyton's band. Because we played mostly for like the new Paramount News.

13.t: Who produced the Grand Terrace shows, and Charlie Carpenter
13.ch: Breakup of Hines band to Lefty Bates
13.q: Maybe after I left. But he was -- the only thing he did while I was with the band was take care of Earl's correspondence. And things like that. Take care of the different businesses.

13.t: The Metropolitan Theater and Erskine Tate's 1929 band
13.s: Personnel and arranging for Tate's orchestra at the Met.
13.ch: Part Two: theaters and the Chicago scene
13.q: Well, there was his brother on trumpet, James Tate. Bob S Hoffner on trumpet, and first part was John Thomas on trombone. Then later on we got Louis Taylor

112.t: Maude deForrest, Gus Smith and the TOBA tab shows
112.s: Gus Smith organizes tab shows through Indiana and Illinois on the TOBA circuit until the girls are sent home and the group returns to New York.
112.q: Well, we had a quartet of youngsters around there. We had Maude deForrest. Later, Maude deForrest went to Europe with Josephine Baker. She had been chosen by Josephine Baker bein' the first strip teaser. Maude deForrest was a very good blues singer. Because she had a heavy voice. And everybody…

112.t: The Club Alabam show: Abbie Mitchell, Eddie Rector, Johnny Hudgins
112.s: Arthur Lyons puts in a big revue that Wooding learned to conduct and that foreshadowed the Cotton Club shows.
112.ch: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
112.q: : Yeah, before that. Because we built up a -- that Fall, like Lyons said, we went in there in May or June, or something like that. That Fall, Arthur Lyons put the show in. This was a great show. We had such stars in that show like Freddie Washington and Abbie Mitchell. And there was Eddie Rec-tor,…

112.t: Eddie Rector's drill, Clarence Robinson and Bunny Weldon staging the show
112.s: He recalls Rector turning the girls' military drill into jazz and the white producer Bunny Weldon telling dancers to grind.
112.ch: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
112.q: But, getting back to this show. We run this show good. We had some legendary people in that show. Because there was Johnny Hodgins and there was Eddie Rector. Eddie Rector was the man that started this coming out of the trenches and different things. And they used his drill today. He created that…

112.t: Winter Garden Sundays and Loew's vaudeville, never the Palace
112.s: Wooding played Sunday concerts at the Winter Garden and Loew's vaudeville but never the Palace until accompanying Rae Harrison.
112.ch: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
112.q: But before that, then Lyons would start playing the Winter Garden. Every Sunday night, we started putting a show into the Winter Garden. I played the Winter Garden I guess, during around a year, I guess about 10 times. Sunday night concerts. And we was doing vaudeville at different times. And we…

112.t: A week at the Lafayette with Chappelle and Stinnette
112.s: The band plays a week at the Lafayette on a bill with Clarence Williams and Eva Taylor, which makes him feel somebody.
112.q: And then the next chance was when I was working -- and then there was an act named CHAPPELLE and STINNETTE. They hired us for a week, in the Lafayette. They hired us for a week in a theater, the Lafayette. On account of what they heard that we was doing a very good job down there.

259.t: Carnival and circus life, a storm that killed performers
259.s: He toured in small shows through Louisiana, Texas and Mississippi, and survived a storm that killed performers by cutting through the tent.
259.q: The women get so nervous, you know, and hollering so, they make him worse than what it is. Mm-hmm.

259.t: Working carnivals and fairs with Joe Roverson
259.s: Vincent describes road carnival and fair work, band size, and the 49 dance where three bands alternated.
259.q: Yeah. He said, who you worked with in carnival? Who? You. Well, my band never was thick as ever on the kind of walking. The last kind of, well, I was still hired. They're taking a job bass band. So I couldn't make it. Romain Emphries was with us then. They said that night we played at the Benitez…

259.t: Jim Kelly and Ernest Kelly, and going to Mexico
259.s: He identifies Jim Kelly as the chambon player in his carnival band, notes Kelly's death from diabetes, and says they went to Mexico together.
259.q: Jim Kelly, yeah. Chambon. That was Ernest Kelly's anchor. We didn't know Ernest Kelly. Didn't have his name either. Yeah, I have his name. He's a trauma. Chambon, yeah. Dead fish brother. He had diabetes. He took me cutting his legs off. Took me apart.

259.t: Jazz Baby, his brother Julius Benson and the Mamie Smith show
259.s: Vincent talks about his brother Julius Benson and Jazz Baby, and a planned show with Mamie Smith that fell through.
259.q: He was a different fella. He was to take us away with a show. Uh huh. Mimmy Smith, you know, which is . Yeah. But then we had packed up and we had to go. But T-Boy and mother and sister didn't want him to go. So after we couldn't take T-Boy, he backed out. We had to back out. So he left there with…

251.s: Albert spells Anise and describes her and her partner as the best dance team he saw.
251.q: A-N-I-S-E, the original Cotton Club, she was a very beautiful girl, a real small, a petite, as they say. And Anise was a little fella, the most beautiful dance team I've ever seen.

251.t: Shadowland Blues, Dixon, and Texas blues singers and TOBA
251.s: On Shadowland Blues, Albert describes the quick same-day recording, Dixon's playing, and traveling blues shows such as Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith at Ella B. Moore's Theater in Dallas, the one TOBA house nearby.
251.ch: Listening to the Troy Floyd records
251.q: The recording companies in those days didn't have too much time to spend with you. Time was in between the solo. Charlie Dixon off the tubo on the trombone. The seventh That's real blues. Yeah. That guy's got a tremendous feeling. Well, he played with all the great blues singers of those days and…

251.s: Floyd's theme was sung and spoken like Ted Lewis; he was more of a gimmick man but could get jobs.
251.ch: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
251.q: Possibly so, more than likely in Texas if you could ever find someone that knew Eddie Perry. Did Troy Floyd have a theme? Yes, Troy's theme was, oh, let's go a little further. You have to come in. I'm afraid. I'm afraid someday you'll leave. I'm afraid someday I'll breathe. I'm afraid. It was a…

251.t: Childhood horn picture and stage acting
251.s: A childhood picture with an old horn, the nickname 1776, and his acting in local stage plays such as Dark Tower.
251.q: Are there any particular questions that you would like to ask me concerning any of the music career or pictures I'd be happy to show them to you? This one here Paul, I'm also somewhat of an actor on the stage. I played in about five or six major productions, that is locally. Was offered a part in…

275.s: He toured with the Freedom Train show in New Orleans, Memphis and St. Louis, where he was a hit.
275.q: Well, that was quite an experience that I had. I traveled with the Freedom Train show and I appeared here in New Orleans, Memphis, and St. Louis. And in St. Louis, I was very well received there on the banks of the Mississippi River where I appeared. I was only scheduled to do three songs and a…

275.t: Blackface, minstrel shows and being the last coon shouter
275.s: He distinguishes blackface from minstrelsy, recalls Kentucky shows, and calls himself the last coon shouter.
275.q: Oh yes, I did blackface, not so much of the minstrel shows as I worked all over the country in theaters and nightclubs as a blackface act. And it's not a minstrel act, it's entirely different in a minstrel. Minstrel, you know, they paint around their lips white and in red blackface you don't do…

275.t: Mae West and her Henderson connection
275.s: He worked with Mae West, relays her Henderson visit in 1909, and tells the 'come up and see me' joke.
275.q: Yes, Mae West, I worked with her and her husband is from Henderson, Kentucky. And she appeared in Henderson before my time, but I was told by my father that she appeared in Henderson back in 1909. Oh for heaven's sakes. With the show there and she had all men in the show but the maid. She never has…

275.t: Working with Mary Martin and Helen Morgan
275.s: He recalls Mary Martin's Broadway shows and nightclub work with Helen Morgan.
275.q: Yes, Mary Martin played in the Broadway show, Louisiana Hayride and also Hollywood Follies. And these other people, I worked with Helen Morgan, too, several times in nightclubs and also taught a girl who went with her show as a course girl.

276.t: Learning 'Big Rock Candy Mountain' on the medicine show; hoboing to Asheville
276.s: After singing 'Big Rock Candy Mountain', Nash says he learned it on a medicine show, hearing it from a West Virginia guitarist. When a show got stranded he hoboed to Asheville, played ukulele at a theater and a club, then returned to New Orleans.
276.ch: Medicine show, hoboing and train songs
276.q: In the months of May, a sunny day, a boyly bum come hiking down the shady land to the sugar can. He was looking for his liking. And he rolled along and he sung a song with a blend of milk and honey. Where a bum can stay for many of days. And he don't need any money. Of the button of the bees and…

276.t: Hobo songs and the 'I'm the bum and you bum the bum' joke
276.s: Nash recalls sad hobo songs sung by men waiting for trains and tells a joke about a bum begging door to door.
276.ch: Medicine show, hoboing and train songs
276.q: Well yeah I heard some guys. Guys should sing. Sing a lot of old sad songs about sitting at the water tank waiting for a train. A lot of them hobo songs they used to sing. Another guy was cracking jokes. So he went to a house and he knocked on the door. The lady said, bum bum you been here before.…

276.t: Reel 2 opening; Kerry Fritz at the Entertainers Cabaret
276.s: Date noted, selling bricks to women, and the entertainer Kerry Fritz and his theme song and repertoire.
276.q: This fellow, Kerry Fritz, he was one of the star entertainers at the Entertainers Cabaret down on Appleville and Franklin at that time.

276.t: Fox, the tap dancer, and meeting him on Canal Street
276.s: Nash recalls the great tap dancer Fox from Algiers and a recent encounter with him, old and rheumatic, sleeping on a newspaper box.
276.q: He was born over there. Well, I bet the people over there would know him. Oh yeah, sure they know him. They know him. And he's one of the old timers, man. He really could dance.

8.t: The Tennessee Ten, Slow Kid and Florence Mills
8.s: The Tennessee Ten show band with Slow Kid, Florence Mills and Peggy Hollander, and a seasick Lake Michigan boat trip.
8.q: On the St. Joe. A big boat. And the last time we made that trip, across that Michigan Lake, that boat cracked us like firecrackers. It was a big boat. And they had a whole well of blue jackets on there. Sailors. Mm-hmm. And you know all them sailors were sick? Mm-hmm. Poor T-Boy is laid out on the…

8.t: Touring with dancer May Elaine on the Orpheum Circuit
8.s: An agent brought Garland's band to Chicago to back May Elaine, a white dancer in blackface who stepped out of a cotton bale, on the Orpheum Circuit for some months.
8.q: When I left there, an agent come and got me to bring a band to Chicago, to play for May Elaine.

8.t: Leaving New Orleans with Mabel Elaine's jazz band show
8.s: Garland describes leaving for Chicago with a stage show, Mabel Elaine and her jazz band, bringing his own New Orleans players; the drummer Happy was nearly left behind.
8.q: How did you happen to leave New Orleans? What happened? Well, Freddie Keppert was playing for a girl by the name they called Mabel Elaine.

8.t: The Tennessee Ten act on the Orpheum Circuit
8.s: Garland left to back the Tennessee Ten act on the Orpheum Circuit, which paid well.
8.q: Yeah. It was on the Orpheum Circuit.

194.s: As a small boy he worked as a kick stunt man in a minstrel show selling CJK medicine, never leaving town.
194.q: Well I was real small. I wasn't doing anything then. I was just trying to make a buck. And they'd use me as a kick stunt man. You know, whenever they had some water to pull on somebody, a pie to batten your feet. That was my job. Wait, did you go out of town with these people on the road? No, I…

194.t: Lollipop Jones, Red Fox and the Dewdrop comedians; dating his early years
194.s: Longhair recalls the comedian Lollipop Jones; the interviewer notes comedians at the Dewdrop; they date the minstrel show to about 1925 and tap dancing to the early 1930s.
194.q: Well, lollipops. I don't know whether you heard of him. Lollipop. Yeah, lollipop Jones. Lollipop Jones in Memphis. Memphis, uh, Lewis. Lewis. Memphis Lewis.

194.s: The song had lyrics about a medicine that would cure everything.
194.q: Really, that's the way it was based upon what it'll do for you. Check your fever, drive away your cold, stop a young man from ever getting old. Nah.

194.t: Champion Jack Dupree and Redd Foxx in the late 1930s
194.s: He met comedian-singer Jack Dupree around 1937-38; they traded piano for singing lessons. Dupree later left town and Fess refused to leave.
194.ch: Early partnerships and career ups and downs
194.q: Well, Red Fox didn't play music. Right. He was just a comedian at that time. And we all stuck together back in the 30s, 33, 37, 38, things started to picking up. Uh, this is when I met Jack Dupree around 1937, 38. And he was a comedian also. He sung the blues and he wore union suits out on the…

53.t: The Baby Mac record, the move north in 1914 and T.O.B.A.
53.s: Billy says he is not the Baby Mac on an Armstrong record. They went to Memphis in 1911, organized a company in New Orleans in 1914 and booked theaters directly to New York; he says they helped organize T.O.B.A. and played it as a singing, dancing, talking team.
53.q: you know. We went to Memphis, Tennessee. Wasn't it, Matt? Yeah. No, we went to Memphis in 1911. 1911. But it was 1914 when we'd come back to New Orleans and organized this company. And then went to New York. Yes. And went everywhere along the lines, stopping in different towns. And at that time, we…

53.t: Writing original material and what their act was
53.s: Billy wrote all their material, which is why they could return often. Mary sang, danced and played leading lady; they did comedy songs together and whole acts.
53.ch: Vaudeville and the name Mac and Mac
53.q: Sure. I used to, in organizing these shows, I'd always sit down and write my material. And so we had, everything we had was original. That's why we could come back and also stay so long whenever we'd play any game. But we always had something new to offer. And I was the originator, see, with her…

53.t: Playing the Lyric Theatre and Robichaux's orchestra
53.s: Where a theater had its own orchestra, theirs played the overture and then the McBrides' band came on stage as part of the show. Robichaux's music was classic, but he enjoyed their style.
53.q: you would just go in and sing? Yes, we did. Now, when we... What did you do? When we go in, uh, uh, so the Lyric, or to any theatre that had a band, well then, their, their band would play their overture, and then our band would come. Oh, you still keep your own band? Oh, sure, yeah.

53.t: Vaudeville in New York: staying on past the first half
53.s: Mary tells how in New York in 1914 they were afraid of being hooked, but kept their act and were held over for weeks at the Lincoln and the Howard. Billy recalls String Beans, Butler May and the Whitman sisters, and how the Northern acts first looked down on them.
53.ch: Vaudeville and the name Mac and Mac
53.q: When you go to New York, you know, you'd get a half of...the first half. Yes. Of the whole...the whole...the first half. And then somebody else had the second half. Well, then instead of us getting just the first half, we'd have the first half. And they'd say, can you change your act for the second…

302.s: He names minstrel shows he toured with, their mixed audiences, and the extra-charge concert after the main show.
302.q: Well, now, the last show, the last minstrel show I was with was, I think that was in 1937. When I was with Brobby Rastus, that's the same show that Bessie Smith was on.

302.s: He explains minstrel one-nighters versus carnival jig shows, tents, trucks and railroad cars, and the concert admission.
302.ch: Minstrel show life and Ida Cox
302.q: Oh, a minstrel show. See, it's different between... A minstrel. A minstrel, you could call it one-nighters. You see, a minstrel played one-nighters. On a carnival show you had a minstrel show too, but they used to call it a jig show.

302.t: Leaving Ida Cox and the Dogtown Scandals show
302.s: He stayed almost a year, left in Huntington, West Virginia; the show had Lonnie Johnson, a bicycle act and chorus girls.
302.ch: Minstrel show life and Ida Cox
302.q: Well, I stayed with Ida almost a year. I left Ida and Charleston, West Virginia. I mean not in Charleston, but in Huntington. We played Charleston and I left from Charleston, we went to Huntington. Yeah. And we played Huntington and I left Ida and Huntington, West Virginia. And I stayed around…

302.t: Touring with Johnny Lee Long on TOBA
302.s: He left in 1926, at nearly sixteen, with Johnny Lee Long's show on the TOBA circuit through southern cities, Chicago and Cincinnati.
302.ch: Early jobs and Johnny Lee Long show
302.q: Well, he used to do a straight. He was a straight man. He used to do a straight. And we was on this TOBA time, the Theatronors Booking Association. We played at towns like Mobile, Birmingham, Atlanta.

15.t: The Plantation Days show and James P. Johnson's band
15.s: Leonard Harper produced the show and James P. Johnson led a ten-to-twelve piece band that played in the pit and on stage.
15.q: Plantation Days. Yeah. You know who launched Deez in New York? No. Barbara Deez? No. Well, he produced it. And, no, I beg your pardon, Leonard Harper. You remember Leonard Harper, don't you? No. That's right, I forget. That's New York. I bet your brother knew. He produced the shows. James P.…

15.t: Interruptions; the show's New York chorus line
15.s: The interviewer complains about noise in the next room, then asks about the show's chorus girls and how the company came together in Chicago.
15.q: Well, we had a couple girls from Chicago, but the Red Bumet, there was about ten girls all together.

15.t: How the Chicago-formed company was booked for Europe; acts in the show
15.s: The show's bulk came from New York but rehearsed in Chicago; Cochran booked it to Europe; Howard names the comedians and Harper and Banks.
15.q: Where did you start to work together? In New York, I mean in Chicago. In Chicago, but the bulk of the show came from New York.

15.t: Stars of the show and James P. as a musician
15.s: Howard lists acts such as the Firecracker Jacks and discusses whether James P. was a trained musician.
15.q: I know where Lombard is. Sure. You know, you knew you write music, you should have a ear. Yeah. Ta-da! Lombard up Telegraph Hill.

369.t: Moms Mabley, Peg Leg Bates and learning to stop a show
369.s: On two theatre dates with the Sweethearts and Moms Mabley she learned from comedians who stopped shows; closers on the bill were the biggest acts.
369.q: She’d put her teeth in the glass, perform, she was a comedian, you know. She’d perform and stop the show. So, that’s how you learn how to stop a show, with performers like that. And then there was another performer, Peg Leg Bates, had one leg. He’d say, “Let me break this other leg for you.”

369.t: Star Time with Lou Holtz and picking numbers that sell
369.s: In the revue Star Time, which ran six to eight weeks, she was the only Black performer; Lou Holtz taught her to walk on stage, and she chose classical-and-jazz numbers that would sell.
369.q: He showed me how to walk out on a stage, Lou Holtz did. And I think he owned a piece of the San Francisco Hotel. But he showed me how to walk out. And he said, “If you give love in your eyes, then you’ll get love in response back.” And I was in the show with him, the Berry brothers got sick so I…

369.t: The chittlin' circuit: Regal, Paradise, Howard and Royal audiences
369.s: She contrasts tough Detroit, the Howard Theatre where classical was unwelcome, and the Royal in Baltimore where a rat was shot; favorite clubs were whichever paid most.
369.q: Detroit was tough. The Howard Theatre was tougher: “Don’t be playin’ any of that classical music here.” And that Royal in Baltimore—the Ink Spots played there once and there was a big rat that ran across the stage. So somebody took out a gun and shot it. They thought it was a cat, you know. And…

369.t: Vaudeville flourishes and vocal impersonations in her act
369.s: Her hip shaking and impersonations of Lena Horne, Nellie Lutcher and Billie Holiday break up the monotony; audiences have a limited attention span.
369.q: I could do Lena Horne and Ella, not Etta Jones, I keep calling her James sometimes. I can do Nellie Lutcher, Rose Murphy and a lot of them; Billie Holiday, especially.

228.t: Authenticity of the play and McLean's acting
228.s: He saw the play as about waiting for the connection, introducing him to theater, and he added lines.
228.ch: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
228.q: Stretched, made for enjoyment, yeah, but it was about that, waiting for the connection to come, because you got something that you need.

228.t: Joining The Connection at the Living Theater
228.s: In 1959 McLean signed with Blue Note and Freddie Redd brought him into the play The Connection, which ran several years and became Shirley Clarke's film.
228.ch: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
228.q: Me, Webster Young, Tony Williams, and Bobby Hutcherson, Grachan Moncur, and Eddie Kahn. I think that was the band that I used there. But it depends. It depended. When ’59 came and I signed with Blue Note – I left Prestige and signed with Blue Note, and then that very same year, the people from the…

228.s: Freddie Redd approved Tina Brooks as McLean's understudy while he took other gigs.
228.ch: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
228.q: Who was – Tina. Tina and I were making records anyway for Blue Note, for Freddie Redd. So I had – Freddie was the musical director. So I had no problem at when when Freddie said, “Jackie, would you mind if Tina was your understudy.” I said, “Hell no, man. I’d love him to be my” – so I would go off…

228.t: Acting with the Living Theater and Julian Beck
228.s: McLean understudied for Living Theater parts, played a Chinese bartender in Paris, and remembers Julian Beck making him up.
228.ch: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
228.q: No. I never got a chance to. I always wanted to. When I was with the Living Theater, they saw that I was very interested in acting and that whole thing. So they always kept me as an understudy for any part. So we’d be like in France or something like that, and one of the guys who was an actor in…

378.t: Recovery, a single in Phoenix and the Flaming Youth Revue
378.s: After typhoid he plays a single in Phoenix, then goes on the circuit with the Flaming Youth Revue.
378.q: Yeah, that's right. Then I finally got well enough and the agent booked me for a couple of dates and that's when I went to -- went to Phoenix, I did a single there. First time I'd ever tried that. My brother was living in Phoenix, the oldest boy, Howard was living in Phoenix there and he was…

378.s: Dance recalls his comic exit routines; Norvo describes the act's three boys and a girl and opening number.
378.q: Yeah. Well those are the things I did in that act -- that Flaming Youth Review was a great act. We had three boys and this little girl. It was a great act. We opened it -- opened it singing, walking across the street -- I can't sing at all, but I just talk, you know --

378.t: Touring the Midwest with the Chautauqua marimba band
378.s: The group of older multi-instrumentalists plays tents in Peru, Indiana, and Lincoln, Illinois, moving every week like a circus.
378.q: Oh, yeah. Yeah. So I got paid, too, you know, I mean it was a job, which I was very happy about.

378.t: End of the Revue; becoming a vaudeville single
378.s: After a year or two with the Revue, he goes out as a xylophone single, usually the number-two act on a vaudeville bill; Dance sets up the life-story thread again.
378.ch: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
378.q: I'd go out and do solos and different type of solo, I was getting away from the -- well other things I was doing, I was trying to be more jazz -- and they were Accepting it a little bit.

89.s: He played B-flat clarinet beside his uncle in the side-show band at eighteen dollars a week, saw armed show people, and did not stay the season.
89.q: Yes, when the circus was playing. Well, that was -- we were the side-show band. I went on the road with them in the side-show band, and I stayed, I think, two months because it was too much for me and -- well, naturally, my vacation was over. It was more of an experience my uncle wanted me to get.

89.t: The Modern Cocktail on the Pantages vaudeville circuit
89.s: He toured Pantages with a five-piece jazz act from Chicago to Seattle, sharing a bill with George Burns.
89.q: Well, yes, it had to go, say, six, about ten ways -- I'd make $5.00, $6.00 maybe a night, something like that, plus -- oh, yeah, I saved quite a bit, saved quite a bit as a youngster then. Then (while in unintelligible) Leroy's -- there was an act out on the road called The Modern Cocktail and…

89.s: He explains TOBA, the black circuit stretching across the South and Midwest, where many acts got their start.
89.ch: Fletcher, Wooding and the Harlem scene
89.q: Bailey's Advice. There was a guy who owned this time called Bailey, but I think it was -- I don't know what the legitimate names -- but TOBA -- that was the black vaudeville circuit, and many, many vaudeville teams originated -- some of them became headliners in the white circuit, some of them…
